en: Chāndogya Upaniṣad: One should meditate upon this syllable "Om" as the Udgītha. For one chants the Udgītha with "Om. Here follows its detailed exposition. 1.1.1.

Of these beings, the earth is the essence; of the earth, water is the essence; of water, plants are the essence; of plants, man is the essence; of man, speech is the essence; of speech, the *Ṛg* is the essence; of the *Ṛg*, the *Sāman* is the essence; of the *Sāman*, the *Udgītha* is the essence. This *Udgītha* is the quintessence of essences, the highest, the supreme, the eighth. || 1.1.2–3 ||

"What is the *ṛc*? What is the *sāman*? What is the *udgītha*?"—thus it is investigated. Speech itself is the *ṛc*; breath is the *sāman*; and this syllable "Om" is the *udgītha*. Now, that which is speech and breath, and the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, is indeed a couple. || 1.1.4–5 ||

This couple is united in this syllable *om*. When a couple comes together, they indeed fulfill each other's desire. He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Udgītha as this syllable, becomes a fulfiller of desires.

This, indeed, is the syllable of assent. For whatever one assents to, one says "Om" to that. Assent is indeed prosperity; he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha, becomes a fulfiller of desires. 1.1.8.

Therefore, this triple knowledge proceeds: with "Om" one causes the announcement; with "Om" one recites the praise; with "Om" one sings the chant. It is for the sake of honoring this very syllable, by its greatness and its essence. 1.1.9.

Therefore, both perform [the ritual]: he who knows this thus, and he who does not know it. But knowledge and ignorance are indeed different. Whatever one performs with knowledge, faith, and the Upaniṣad—that alone becomes more powerful. Thus, indeed, is the further explanation of this very syllable. 1.1.10.
Thus ends the first section.
Once, when the gods and the asuras—both of whom were offspring of Prajāpati—were contending with one another, the gods took up the Udgītha, thinking, "By means of this, we shall overcome them. 1.2.1.
They meditated upon the breath of the nose as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore, one smells both the fragrant and the foul with it, for it has been pierced by evil. 1.2.2.
Then they meditated upon speech as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore, by means of that [speech], one speaks both the true and the false; for it has been pierced by evil. 1.2.3.
Then they venerated the eye as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore, by means of it, one sees both the beautiful and the ugly, for it has been pierced by evil. 1.2.4.

Then they meditated upon the ear as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore, by means of it, one hears both what is worth hearing and what is not worth hearing; for it has been pierced by evil. 1.2.5.

Then they meditated upon the mind as the Udgītha. The Asuras pierced it with evil. Therefore, by means of it, one intends both that which is to be intended and that which is not to be intended; for it has been pierced by evil. 1.2.6.

Then, they meditated upon that very breath which is the principal one in the mouth as the Udgītha. When the Asuras struck it, they were shattered, just as a clod of earth would shatter upon striking a solid stone. Just as a clod of earth shatters upon striking a solid stone, even so does he shatter who desires evil against one who knows this, and whoever seeks to harm him; for such a person is like a solid stone. By means of this [breath], one perceives neither fragrance nor foul odor, for it is free from evil. Whatever one eats and whatever one drinks by means of it, thereby one sustains the other vital breaths. Indeed, at the end, one departs after having found this very [breath]; thus, at the end, one simply opens the mouth wide.

Aṅgiras meditated upon that as the Udgītha. Indeed, they consider this very one to be Aṅgiras, for he is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs (*aṅga*). With that, Bṛhaspati meditated upon him as the Udgītha. Indeed, they consider this very one to be Bṛhaspati; for speech is the Great One (*bṛhatī*), and he is its lord (*pati*). With that, Ayāsya meditated upon him as the Udgītha. Indeed, they consider this very one to be Ayāsya, for he moves forth (*ayate*) from the mouth (*āsya*). With that, Baka Dālbhya came to know him. He became the Udgātṛ priest for the Naimiśīyas. He used to obtain desires for them by singing. Verily, one becomes a singer of desires who, knowing it thus, meditates upon this syllable as the Udgītha. This is with reference to the self (*adhyātma*).
Thus ends the second section.

Now, with reference to the deities: one should meditate upon that very sun which shines as the Udgītha. Indeed, rising, he sings the Udgītha for the sake of all creatures; rising, he drives away darkness and fear. He who knows this becomes indeed a dispeller of fear and darkness. 1.3.1.

This one here and that one yonder are indeed the same. This one is warm, and that one is warm. People call this one "sound" (*svara*), and they call that one "sound" (*svara*) and "echo" (*pratyāsvara*). Therefore, one should meditate upon both this one and that one as the *udgītha*. 1.3.2.

Now, one should indeed meditate upon the *vyāna* as the *udgītha*. That which one breathes out is the *prāṇa*; that which one breathes in is the *apāna*. Now, that which is the junction (*saṃdhi*) of the *prāṇa* and the *apāna* is the *vyāna*. What is the *vyāna*, that is speech. Therefore, one utters speech without breathing out or breathing in. (1.3.3) What is speech, that is the *ṛc*. Therefore, one utters the *ṛc* without breathing out or breathing in. What is the *ṛc*, that is the *sāman*. Therefore, one sings the *sāman* without breathing out or breathing in. What is the *sāman*, that is the *udgītha*. Therefore, one sings the *udgītha* without breathing out or breathing in. (1.3.4) For this reason, whatever other vigorous actions there are—such as the churning of fire, the running in a race, or the drawing of a strong bow—one performs them without breathing out or breathing in. For this very cause, one should meditate upon the *vyāna* as the *udgītha*. (1.3.5)

Now, one should meditate upon the syllables of the *udgītha*: "ut," "gī," and "tha. "Ut" is indeed breath (*prāṇa*), for by means of breath one rises up. "Gī" is speech (*vāc*); for they call speech "giraḥ. "Tha" is food (*anna*); for on food all this is established. Alternatively: "Ut" is heaven; "gī" is the intermediate space; "tha" is the earth. "Ut" is the sun; "gī" is the wind; "tha" is fire. "Ut" is the Sāmaveda; "gī" is the Yajurveda; "tha" is the Ṛgveda. For him who knows these syllables of the *udgītha* thus and meditates upon them as "ut," "gī," and "tha," speech yields its milk—the milk of speech—and he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food. 1.3.6–7.

Now, indeed, there is the fulfillment of one's prayer. One should perform the approach (*upasaraṇa*) thus: one should approach that *sāman* with which one intends to chant the praise; [1.3.8] one should approach that *ṛc* in which [the *sāman* is based], that *ṛṣi* who is its seer (*ārṣeya*), and that deity whom one intends to praise; [1.3.9] one should approach that *chandas* (meter) with which one intends to chant the praise; one should approach that *stoma* (hymnic formation) with which one is about to chant the praise; [1.3.10] one should approach that direction toward which one intends to chant the praise. [1.3.11] Having finally approached oneself, one should chant the praise while meditating on the desired object, being vigilant. For it is close at hand that the desired object for which one chants the praise shall be fulfilled—for the desired object for which one chants the praise shall be fulfilled. [1.3.12]
Thus ends the third section.

One should meditate upon this syllable *om* as the Udgītha. For one begins the chant with *om*. Here follows its detailed explanation. The gods, indeed, fearing death, entered the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*). They concealed themselves by means of the meters (*chandas*). Because they concealed themselves by means of these, that is the "meter-ness" (*chandastva*) of the meters. There, death watched for them just as one might watch for a fish in water; he watched for them in the *Ṛc*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*. But they, having discovered him, ascended above the *Ṛc*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*, and entered the very tone (*svara*). Whenever one reaches the *Ṛc*, one utters the tone *om*; likewise the *Sāman*, likewise the *Yajus*. This tone is this very syllable; it is immortal and fearless. Having entered it, the gods became immortal.
He who, knowing this thus, utters the syllable *praṇava*, enters that very syllable—tone, immortal, and fearless. Having entered it, he becomes immortal, even as the gods are immortal. 1.4.5.
Thus ends the fourth section.
Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha. Yonder sun, verily, is the Udgītha; he is the Praṇava, for he goes along sounding "Om. 1.5.1.

"It was precisely this that I praised; therefore you are my only son," Kauṣītaki said to his son. "You must turn back the rays; then indeed many sons shall be yours. Thus with respect to the deities. 1.5.2.

Now, with reference to the self: one should meditate upon that which is the principal breath (*prāṇa*) as the *udgītha*. For it moves along sounding "Om. Kauṣītaki said to his son: "I sang this very thing; therefore, you are my only [son]. "You, however, should sing to the breaths as a plurality, for then many sons will indeed be mine," he said.

Now, indeed, that which is the Udgītha is the Praṇava; that which is the Praṇava is the Udgītha. For even from the seat of the Hotṛ-priest, one may rectify a poorly performed Udgītha—yes, one may rectify it. 1.5.5.
Thus ends the fifth section.

This [earth] is the *ṛc*; Agni is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. This [earth] is *sā*; Agni is *ama*; that is the *sāman*. The intermediate space is the *ṛc*; Vāyu is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. The intermediate space is *sā*; Vāyu is *ama*; that is the *sāman*. The sky is the *ṛc*; Āditya is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. The sky is *sā*; Āditya is *ama*; that is the *sāman*. The stars are the *ṛc*; the Moon is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. The stars are *sā*; the Moon is *ama*; that is the *sāman*.

Now, that which is the white light of the sun is the *ṛc*; and that which is the blue, the exceedingly dark [light] is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is mounted upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being mounted upon the *ṛc*. Now, that which is the white light of the sun is indeed *sā*; and that which is the blue, the exceedingly dark [light] is *ama*. That is the *sāman*. Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, from the nails on to the tips of his toes entirely golden— His eyes are like a lotus flower that has the color of a monkey’s anus. His name is "Ut" (the Risen). He has risen above all evils. Indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils. The *ṛc* and the *sāman* are his two joints (*geṣṇau*). Therefore, he is the *udgītha* (the High Chant). And for that reason, the *udgātṛ* (the chanter) is so called, for he is the singer of this [person]. He rules over those worlds that are beyond the sun and over the desires of the gods. Thus far with respect to the divine.
Thus ends the sixth section.

Now with reference to the self: speech is indeed the *ṛc*, and breath is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. Speech is *sā*, and breath is *ama*; that together is the *sāman*. 1.7.1.

The eye is indeed the *ṛc*; the self (*ātman*) is the *sāman*. This *sāman* is thus supported upon this *ṛc*. Therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. The eye is indeed the *sā*; the self is the *ama*. That is the *sāman*. 1.7.2.

The ear is indeed the *ṛc*, and the mind is the *sāman*. Thus, this *sāman* is supported upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as being supported upon the *ṛc*. The ear is indeed the *sā*, and the mind is the *ama*; that is the *sāman*. 1.7.3.

Now, that which is the white light of the eye is the *ṛc*; and that which is the blue, the exceedingly black, is the *sāman*. This *sāman* rests upon this *ṛc*; therefore, the *sāman* is sung as resting upon the *ṛc*. Now, that which is the white light of the eye is indeed *sā*; and that which is the blue, the exceedingly black, is *ama*; that is the *sāman*. 1.7.4.

Now, this person who is seen within the eye—he is the Ṛg, he is the Sāman, he is the Uktha, he is the Yajus, he is the Brahman. His form is the very same as the form of that [other person in the sun]; his two joints are the two joints of that; his name is the same as the name of that. 1.7.5.

He is the lord of those worlds that are on this side of it, and of the desires of men. Therefore, when these people sing to the lute, they sing to him; hence they are winners of wealth. Now, he who, knowing this thus, sings the Sāman, sings to both [sets of worlds]. By means of that [upper world], he attains those worlds which are beyond it, as well as the desires of the gods. And by means of this [lower world], he attains those worlds which are on this side of it, as well as the desires of men. Therefore, an Udgātṛ priest who knows this should say: "What desire shall I obtain for you by singing? For he who, knowing this thus, sings the Sāman, is indeed the master of obtaining desires through his singing—yes, he who sings the Sāman.
Thus ends the seventh section.

There were three men who were skilled in the *udgītha*: Śilaka Śālāvatya, Caikitāyana Dālbhya, and Pravāhaṇa Jaibali. They said, "We are indeed skilled in the *udgītha*; come, let us have a discussion on the *udgītha*. Saying "So be it," they sat down together. Then Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said, "Let the two venerable ones speak first; I shall listen to the speech of two Brahmins as they speak."
Then Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya, "Come, let me question you. "Ask," he replied. 1.8.3.

"What is the goal of the Sāman? "Its goal is tone," he said. "What is the goal of tone? "Its goal is breath," he said. "What is the goal of breath? "Its goal is food," he said. "What is the goal of food? "Its goal is water," he said. 1.8.4.

"What is the goal of the waters? "That world," he said. "What is the goal of that world? "One must not lead beyond the heavenly world," he said. "We establish the Sāman upon the heavenly world, for the Sāman has the heavenly world as its praise. || 1.8.5 ||

Śilaka Śālāvatya said to Caikitāyana Dālbhya: "O Dālbhya, your Sāman is indeed without a foundation. If someone were to say to you now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would surely fall off. 1.8.6.

"Come, let me learn this from your reverence," he said. "Learn it," he replied. "What is the goal of that world? "This world," he said. "What is the goal of this world? "One must not lead beyond the world that is the foundation," he said. "We establish the Sāman upon the world that is the foundation, for the Sāman has the foundation as its basis. || 1.8.7 ||

Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him: "O Śālāvatya, your Sāman is indeed finite. If someone were to say now, 'Your head shall fall off,' your head would indeed fall off. Come, let me learn this from your reverence. "Learn it," he said. 1.8.8.
Thus ends the eighth section.

"What is the goal of this world? "Space," he said. "Indeed, all these beings arise from space alone; they dissolve back into space. Space is indeed greater than these; space is the ultimate resort. 1.9.1

This is that Udgītha which is higher than the high; it is infinite. For one who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the Udgītha as higher than the high, there comes to be what is higher than the high, and he conquers worlds that are higher than the high. 1.9.2.

Atidhanvā Śaunaka, having taught this very Udgītha to Udaraśāṇḍilya, said: "As long as they shall know this Udgītha among their offspring, so long will there be for them a superior life in this world; and likewise in the other world, a world. He who, knowing it thus, worships it—for him there is indeed a superior life in that other world, and likewise in the other world, a world, a world. 1.9.3–4.
Thus ends the ninth section.

When the Kurus had been destroyed by hailstorms, Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa lived as a wandering beggar with his wife Āṭikī in the village of a wealthy man. He begged some boiled beans from the wealthy man who was eating them. The man said to him, "There are no others than these which are set before me. "Give me some of these," he said. The man gave them to him. "Here, drink some water too," [the man offered]. "If I were to drink, it would be drinking what has been left over by another," he replied. "But are not these beans also left over? [the man asked]. "I certainly would not have survived if I had not eaten these," he replied. "Water is for my own pleasure."

Having eaten, he brought the leftovers to his wife. Even before they were consumed, she became well-supplied with food. She accepted them and set them aside. Then, as he was rising in the morning, he said: "If only we could obtain some food! We might then obtain a measure of wealth. This king is going to perform a sacrifice; he will choose me for all the priestly offices."

His wife said to him, "Come now, eat these very beans. Having eaten them, he went to that sacrifice which was being performed. There, he sat down near the Udgātṛ priests as they were about to chant the Stotra in the place of chanting. He said to the Prastotṛ: "O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Prastāva, your head will fall off. In the same way, he said to the Udgātṛ: "O Udgātṛ, if you chant the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Udgītha, your head will fall off. In the same way, he said to the Pratihartṛ: "O Pratihartṛ, if you chant the Pratihāra without knowing the deity that is inherent in the Pratihāra, your head will fall off. Terrified, they remained silent.
Thus ends the tenth section.
Then the sacrificer said to him: "I desire to know you, O Blessed One. He replied, "I am Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa. 1.11.1.

He said, "I have indeed sought you, O Blessed One, for all these priestly offices (*ārtvijya*). It was because I did not know of you that I chose others. Let the Blessed One himself perform all the priestly offices for me. "So be it," he replied. "In that case, let these very priests praise [the sacrifice] with my permission; however, you must give me as much wealth as you would give to them. "So be it," the sacrificer replied.

Then the Prastotṛ approached him and said: "Venerable sir, you told me, 'O Prastotṛ, if you chant the Prastāva without knowing the deity that is connected with the Prastāva, your head will fall off. Which is that deity? 1.11.4.

"It is *prāṇa*," he said. "Indeed, all these beings enter into *prāṇa* alone and emerge from *prāṇa* alone. This deity is connected with the *prastāva*. Had you chanted the *prastāva* without knowing it, your head would have fallen off at my word. (1.11.5)

Then the Udgātṛ approached him and said: "Venerable sir, you told me, 'If you chant the Udgītha without knowing the deity that is associated with the Udgītha, your head will shatter. Which is that deity? 1.11.6.

"It is Āditya," he said. "Indeed, all these beings sing to Āditya as he is high above. This deity is connected with the Udgītha. If you had sung the Udgītha without knowing it, your head would have fallen off, as was said by me. 1.11.7.

Then the Pratihartṛ approached him and said: "Venerable sir, you told me, 'O Pratihartṛ, if you perform the Pratihāra without knowing the deity that is associated with the Pratihāra, your head will shatter. Which is that deity? 1.11.8

"Food," he said. "For indeed, all these beings live by taking up food alone. This deity is connected with the *pratihāra*. If you had performed the *pratihāra* without knowing it, your head would have fallen off—just as was said by me, 'just as was said by me. 1.11.9.
Thus ends the eleventh section.

Now, therefore, follows the *udgītha* of the dogs. Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—went out to recite his private Vedic study. To him appeared a white dog. Other dogs approached it and said, "Venerable sir, sing for us food; we are hungry. He said to them, "Come to me right here in the morning. Then Baka Dālbhya—or Glāva Maitreya—waited there. They came running together just as those who are about to chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* hymn run forward, holding onto one another. Having sat down together, they uttered the sound *hiṃ*. "Oṃ! We have eaten! Oṃ! We shall drink! Oṃ! May the god Varuṇa, Prajāpati, Savitṛ, bring food here! O Lord of Food, bring food here! Oṃ!"* 1.12.1–5.
Thus ends the twelfth section.

This world, indeed, is the syllable *hāu*; the wind is the syllable *hāi*; the moon is the syllable *atha*; the self (*ātman*) is the syllable *iha*; fire is the syllable *ī*. (1.13.1) The sun is the syllable *ū*; invocation (*nihava*) is the syllable *e*; the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*) are the syllable *au-ho-ī*; Prajāpati is the syllable *hiṃ*; breath (*prāṇa*) is the tone (*svara*); food is the syllable *yā*; speech is the *virāj*. (1.13.2) The thirteenth is the unexpressed (*anirukta*) chant (*stobha*), the moving (*saṃcara*) syllable *huṃ*. (1.13.3) Speech yields its milk for him who knows this secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the Sāmans—the milk that is the yield of speech. He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food, he who knows this secret doctrine of the Sāmans, who knows the secret doctrine. (1.13.4)
Thus ends the thirteenth section.
Thus ends the first chapter.
The worship of the entire Sāman is indeed good. For that which is good, they call "Sāman"; that which is not good, they call "Asāman. 2.1.1.

Regarding this, they also say: "He has approached him with *sāman*"; by this they mean, "He has approached him with what is good. Or they say: "He has approached him without *sāman*"; by this they mean, "He has approached him with what is not good. (2.1.2)

Now they also say: "It is *sāman* for us, alas! when something is good; they mean "it is indeed good" by that. "It is not *sāman* for us, alas! when something is not good; they mean "it is indeed not good" by that. (2.1.3)
He who, knowing this thus, venerates the Sāman as "the good"—verily, it is close at hand that good dharmas should come to him and bow down before him. 2.1.4.
Thus ends the first section.

One should meditate upon the Sāman as fivefold in the worlds: the earth is the *hiṃkāra*, fire is the *prastāva*, the intermediate space is the *udgītha*, the sun is the *pratihāra*, and the sky is the *nidhana*. Thus with respect to those that are above. 2.2.1.

Now, regarding the unobstructed [elements]: heaven is the *hiṃkāra*, the sun is the *prastāva*, the intermediate space is the *udgītha*, fire is the *pratihāra*, and the earth is the *nidhana*. 2.2.2.
The worlds, both ascending and descending, become favorable to him who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the worlds. 2.2.3.
Thus ends the second section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in rain. The preceding wind is the *hiṅkāra*; the cloud arises, that is the *prastāva*; it rains, that is the *udgītha*; it lightens and thunders, that is the *pratihāra*; it ceases, that is the *nidhana*. 2.3.1.
It rains for him, indeed it rains for him, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in rain. 2.3.2.
Thus ends the third section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters. That which is the gathering of clouds is the *hiṃkāra*; that which rains is the *prastāva*; those [rivers] which flow eastward are the *udgītha*; those which flow westward are the *pratihāra*; and the ocean is the *nidhana*. 2.4.1.
He does not perish in water; he becomes possessed of water—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in all waters. 2.4.2.
Thus ends the fourth section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons: Spring is the *hiṃkāra*, Summer is the *prastāva*, the Rainy season is the *udgītha*, Autumn is the *pratihāra*, and Winter is the *nidhana*. 2.5.1.
The seasons serve him; he becomes possessed of the seasons—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in the seasons. 2.5.2.
Thus ends the fifth section.
One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman in animals: goats are the *hiṃkāra*, sheep are the *prastāva*, cows are the *udgītha*, horses are the *pratihāra*, and man is the *nidhana*. 2.6.1.
Cattle come to him and he becomes rich in cattle, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman in cattle. 2.6.2.
Thus ends the sixth section.

One should meditate upon the fivefold Sāman that is progressively higher and more excellent within the vital breaths. Breath is the *hiṃkāra*; speech is the *prastāva*; sight is the *udgītha*; hearing is the *pratihāra*; and mind is the *nidhana*. These are indeed progressively higher and more excellent. 2.7.1.

"Superior and more excellent becomes his lot, and he conquers superior and more excellent worlds—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the fivefold Sāman as 'superior and more excellent' within the vital breaths. Thus far for the fivefold [Sāman]. 2.7.2.
Thus ends the seventh section.

Now, regarding the sevenfold [Sāman]: one should meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech. Whatever in speech is "hum," that is the *hiṃkāra*. What is "pra," that is the *prastāva*. What is "ā," that is the *ādi* || 2.8.1 || What is "ud," that is the *udgītha*. What is "prati," that is the *pratihāra*. What is "upa," that is the *upadrava*. What is "ni," that is the *nidhana* || 2.8.2 ||
Speech milks for him that milk which is the milk of speech; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the sevenfold Sāman in speech. 2.8.3.
Thus ends the eighth section.

Now, one should indeed meditate upon this sun as the sevenfold Sāman. It is "Sāman" because it is always the same (*sama*); it is "Sāman" because it is the same toward everyone, thinking, "toward me, toward me. (2.9.1) One should know that all these beings are dependent upon it. That which is before its rising is the *hiṃkāra*. Upon it the domestic animals depend; therefore they make the sound *hiṃ*. For they partake of the *hiṃkāra* of this Sāman. (2.9.2)

Now, that which occurs at the first rising [of the sun] is the *prastāva* (the introductory chant). Therefore, human beings are dependent upon it; for this reason, they are desirous of undertaking and desirous of praise, for they partake in this *sāman* through the *prastāva*. 2.9.3.

Now, that which occurs at the time of the gathering of cattle (*saṃgava-velā*) is its *ādi* (the beginning). To it birds are attached; therefore, they fly about in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) without any support, holding themselves up by means of it, for they partake in the *ādi* of this Sāman. 2.9.4.

Now, that which is exactly at midday is the *udgītha*. To it the gods are attached; therefore they are the best among the offspring of Prajāpati, for they are the sharers in the *udgītha* of this Sāman. 2.9.5.

Now, that which comes after midday and before afternoon is the *pratihāra*. To it, embryos are attached; therefore, they are held back and do not fall away, for they partake in this *sāman*’s *pratihāra*. 2.9.6.

Now, that which follows the afternoon and precedes sunset is the *upadrava* (the distressing part). To this belong the forest animals (*āraṇyāḥ*). Therefore, when they see a man, they flee into the brush or into holes, crying out "upadrava! (distress!), for they are participants in this *sāman*. 2.9.7.

Now, that which occurs when [the sun] has just set is the *nidhana*; the ancestors are dependent upon that part of it. Therefore, they lay them down [in the grave], for they are sharers in the *nidhana* of this Sāman. Thus, indeed, one meditates upon yonder sun as the sevenfold Sāman. 2.9.8.
Thus ends the ninth section.

Now, one should indeed meditate upon the sevenfold Sāman as being commensurate with oneself and transcending death. *Hiṃkāra* consists of three syllables; *Prastāva* consists of three syllables. That is equal. 2.10.1.
"Ādi" consists of two syllables; "pratihāra" consists of four syllables. Therefore, one [syllable] is added here; thus, it is equal. 2.10.2
"Udgītha" has three syllables; "upadrava" has four syllables. With three syllables each, they become equal. One syllable remains over, making [the total] three syllables. That is equal. (2.10.3)

“Nidhana” consists of three syllables; thus, it becomes equal [to the preceding]. These, indeed, are twenty-two syllables. (2.10.4) By twenty-one, one attains the Āditya; for that Āditya is the twenty-first from here. With the twenty-second, one conquers what is beyond the Āditya. That is the vault of heaven (*nāka*); that is free from sorrow (*viśoka*). (2.10.5)

He attains victory over the sun in this world; indeed, there is for him a victory even beyond the victory over the sun, who, knowing this thus, meditates upon the sevenfold Sāman as commensurate with the self and transcending death—yes, he meditates upon the Sāman. 2.10.6.
Thus ends the tenth section.
The mind is the *hiṃkāra*; speech is the *prastāva*; the eye is the *udgītha*; the ear is the *pratihāra*; the breath is the *nidhana*. This *Gāyatra* chant is woven into the vital breaths. 2.11.1.

He who thus knows this Gāyatra woven upon the vital breaths becomes possessed of vital breaths; he reaches a full lifespan; he lives radiantly; he becomes great in offspring and cattle; he becomes great in fame. He should be high-minded; that is his vow. 2.11.2.
Thus ends the eleventh section.

When one rubs [the fire-sticks] together, that is the *hiṃkāra*. When smoke arises, that is the *prastāva*. When it blazes, that is the *udgītha*. When there are embers, that is the *pratihāra*. When it subsides, that is the *nidhana*; when it is completely extinguished, that is the *nidhana*. This is the *rathaṃtara* chant woven into the fire. 2.12.1.

He who thus knows this Rathantara chant as woven into the fire becomes endowed with spiritual luster, becomes an eater of food, reaches a full lifespan, lives radiantly, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He must not rinse his mouth toward the fire, nor spit toward it; that is his vow. 2.12.2.
Thus ends the twelfth section.

When he makes an invitation, that is the *hiṃkāra*. When he makes himself known, that is the *prastāva*. When he lies with a woman, that is the *udgītha*. When he lies with her in return, that is the *pratihāra*. When he passes the time, that is the *nidhana*. When he reaches the end, that is the *nidhana*. This is the Vāmadevya [Sāman] woven upon the couple. 2,13.1.

He who thus knows this Vāmadevya [Sāman] as woven upon the couple becomes a couple himself; he procreates from every couple; he reaches a full lifespan; he lives radiantly; he becomes great in offspring and cattle; he becomes great in fame. He should not avoid anyone [in sexual intercourse]. That is his vow. 2.13.2.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

The rising sun is the *hiṅkāra*; the risen sun is the *prastāva*; midday is the *udgītha*; the afternoon is the *pratihāra*; and the setting sun is the *nidhana*. This is the Bṛhat Sāman woven into the sun. 2.14.1.

He who thus knows this Bṛhat as woven upon the sun becomes radiant and an eater of food; he reaches a full lifespan, lives long, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not revile the burning [sun]. That is his vow.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

The clouds gather—that is the *hiṃkāra*. The cloud is born—that is the *prastāva*. It rains—that is the *udgītha*. It flashes and thunders—that is the *pratihāra*. It ceases—that is the *nidhana*. This is the Vairūpa [Sāman] woven upon Parjanya. 2.15.1.

He who thus knows this Vairūpa [Sāman] as woven into Parjanya secures cattle that are both deformed and well-formed; he reaches a full lifespan, lives long, becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not revile it when it rains. That is the observance. 2.15.2.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.

Spring is the *hiṃkāra*, summer is the *prastāva*, the rainy season is the *udgītha*, autumn is the *pratihāra*, and winter is the *nidhana*. This is the Vairāja [Sāman] woven upon the seasons. 2.16.1.

He who thus knows this Vairāja [Sāman] as woven upon the seasons shines forth with offspring, with cattle, and with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). He reaches a full lifespan; he lives long; he becomes great in offspring and cattle, and great in fame. He should not revile the seasons. That is his vow. 2.16.2.
Thus ends the sixteenth section.

The earth is the *hiṃkāra*; the intermediate space is the *prastāva*; the sky is the *udgītha*; the quarters are the *pratihāra*; the ocean is the *nidhana*. These are the *śakvarī* verses woven into the worlds. 2.17.1.

He who thus knows these Śakvarī verses as woven upon the worlds becomes possessed of the worlds; he reaches a full lifespan; he lives radiantly; he becomes great in offspring and cattle; he becomes great in fame. He should not revile the worlds—that is his vow. 2.17.2.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
Goats are the *hiṃkāra*; sheep are the *prastāva*; cows are the *udgītha*; horses are the *pratihāra*; man is the *nidhana*. These are the *revatī* verses woven into animals. 2.18.1.

He who thus knows these Revatī verses as interwoven with cattle becomes possessed of cattle; he reaches a full lifespan; he lives long; he becomes great in offspring and cattle; he becomes great in fame. He should not revile cattle. That is his vow. 2.18.2.
Thus ends the eighteenth section.
The hair is the *hiṃkāra*; the skin is the *prastāva*; the flesh is the *udgītha*; the bone is the *pratihāra*; the marrow is the *nidhana*. This *yajñāyajñīya* chant is woven into the limbs. 2.19.1.

He who thus knows this Yajñāyajñīya as woven into the limbs becomes possessed of limbs; he does not suffer from any deficiency of limb; he reaches a full lifespan; he lives radiantly; he becomes great in offspring and cattle; he becomes great in fame. He should not eat marrow for a year—that is the vow—or rather, he should simply not eat marrow. 2.19.2.
Thus ends the nineteenth section.
Agni is the *hiṃkāra*; Vāyu is the *prastāva*; Āditya is the *udgītha*; the constellations are the *pratihāra*; the Moon is the *nidhana*. This is the Rājana chant woven into the deities. 2.20.1.

He who thus knows this King woven into the deities attains the same world, the same origin, and union with these very deities. He reaches a full lifespan; he lives radiantly; he becomes great in offspring and cattle; he becomes great in fame. He should not revile Brahmins—that is his vow. 2.20.2.
Thus ends the twentieth section.

The triple knowledge is the *hiṅkāra*; these three worlds are the *prastāva*; fire, wind, and the sun are the *udgītha*; the stars, birds, and rays of light are the *pratihāra*; serpents, Gandharvas, and ancestors are the *nidhana*. This Sāman is woven throughout everything. 2.21.1.
He who knows this Sāman thus woven into everything becomes everything itself. Regarding this, there is this verse:
"There are those which are fivefold, three by three; there is nothing greater or higher than them.
He who knows that becomes all; from all directions, they bring tribute to him."
"One should worship with the thought, 'I am all. That is the vow; that is the vow. (2.21.4)
Thus ends the twenty-first section.

"I choose the roaring Sāman, which is beneficial for cattle"—this is the *udgītha* of Agni. That which is undefined belongs to Prajāpati; that which is defined belongs to Soma. That which is soft and smooth belongs to Vāyu; that which is smooth and powerful belongs to Indra; that which is like the cry of a crane belongs to Bṛhaspati; that which is hoarse belongs to Varuṇa. One should employ all of these, but one should avoid that which belongs to Varuṇa. 2.22.1.

"May I sing forth immortality for the gods," thus he should sing; "the ancestral offering for the fathers, hope for men, grass and water for animals, the heavenly world for the sacrificer, and food for myself"—meditating on these in his mind, he should chant with vigilance. 2.22.2.

All vowels are the self of Indra; all sibilants (ūṣman) are the self of Prajāpati; all consonants (sparśa) are the self of Death. If someone should find fault with him regarding the vowels, he should say to that person: "I have sought refuge in Indra; he will answer you. (2.22.3) Now, if someone should find fault with him regarding the sibilants, he should say to that person: "I have sought refuge in Prajāpati; he will look upon you [with indifference]. Now, if someone should find fault with him regarding the consonants, he should say to that person: "I have sought refuge in Death; he will burn you up. (2.22.4)

All vowels should be pronounced with resonance and strength, thinking, "I bestow strength upon Indra. All sibilants should be pronounced unswallowed, unexpelled, and open, thinking, "I surrender my self to Prajāpati. All stops should be pronounced with slight [contact] and not pressed together, thinking, "I avoid surrendering my self to Death. || 2.22.5 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second section.

There are three branches of duty: sacrifice, study, and charity constitute the first; austerity alone is the second; and the third is the student who dwells in the house of his teacher, exhausting himself completely in the service of the teacher’s household. All these attain worlds of merit; he who is established in Brahman attains immortality. 2.23.1.

Prajāpati brooded over the worlds. From them, thus brooded over, the threefold knowledge issued forth. He brooded over that; from it, thus brooded over, these syllables issued forth: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *svar*. (2.23.2) He brooded over them; from them, thus brooded over, the syllable *oṃ* issued forth. Just as all leaves are pierced by a stalk, so is all speech pierced by the syllable *oṃ*. The syllable *oṃ* is indeed all this; the syllable *oṃ* is indeed all this. (2.23.3)
Thus ends the twenty-third section.

The exponents of Brahman say: "The morning pressing belongs to the Vasus, the midday pressing to the Rudras, and the third pressing to the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas. (2.24.1) "In that case, where is the world of the sacrificer? If one does not know this, how could he perform the sacrifice? Only one who knows it should perform it. (2.24.2)
Formerly, before the commencement of the Prātaranuvāka, having sat down behind the Gārhapatya fire facing north, he sings the Vāsava Sāman.
"Open the door to the world! May we behold you, O Radiant One, for the sake of the sacrifice! (2.24.4)

Then he offers an oblation: "Homage to Agni, the dweller on earth, the dweller in the world! Find a world for me, the sacrificer! This indeed is the world of the sacrificer; I am in this. Here, beyond his lifespan, svāhā! Having said, "Remove the crossbar," he rises. To him the Vasus present the morning pressing.
Formerly, before the commencement of the midday pressing, he sits down behind the Āgnīdhrīya fire facing north and sings the Sāman dedicated to Rudra.
"Unveil the door to the world! May we behold you, O Vira! Hūm!

Then he offers: "Homage to Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space, who dwells in the world! Find a world for me, the sacrificer! This indeed is the world of the sacrificer; I am in this [world]. Here, after his life has passed, svāhā! Having said, "Remove the crossbar," he stands up. To him, the Rudras hand over the midday pressing.

Formerly, before the commencement of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), having sat down behind the Āhavanīya fire facing north, he sings the *Sāman* dedicated to Āditya and that dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
"Open the door to the world! May we behold you, O Self-radiant One! Huṃ! Ā! Jyā! Yo! Ā! 2-1-1-1! Thus [he worships] the Sun. 2.24.12.
Now follows the Vaiśvadeva: "Open the door to the worlds! May we behold you with the Sāman! Huṃ! Ā! Jyā! Yo! Ā! 2-1-1! (2.24.13)

Then he offers the oblation: "Homage to the Ādityas and to all the gods who dwell in heaven, who dwell in the world! Find a world for me, the sacrificer! (2.24.14) "This indeed is the world of the sacrificer; here I am, the sacrificer, beyond the span of life, svāhā! Having said, "Strike away the crossbar," he rises. (2.24.15)
Therefore, both the Ādityas and the Viśvedevas bestow the third libation upon him. He indeed knows the measure of the sacrifice who knows this—yea, who knows this. 2.24.16.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section.
Thus ends the second chapter.
Yonder sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods. Of it, the sky is the cross-beam; the intermediate space is the cake; and the rays are the sons. 3.1.1.

Those rays of his which go eastward are its eastern honey-cells; the *Ṛg* verses are the honey-makers, and the *Ṛgveda* itself is the flower. Those [verses] are indeed immortal waters. These very *Ṛg* verses heated this *Ṛgveda*. From it, thus heated, there was produced as its essence (*rasa*) fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. That flowed out; it took refuge around the sun. That, indeed, is this red form of the sun.
Thus ends the first section.

Now, those rays of his that are to the south are his southern honey-cells; the Yajus formulas themselves are the honey-makers; the Yajurveda itself is the flower; and those are the immortal waters. These very Yajus formulas heated this Yajurveda. From it, thus heated, there was produced as its essence (rasa) fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. That flowed forth; it took refuge around the sun. That, indeed, is this bright form of the sun.
Thus ends the second section.

Now, those rays of his that point westward are his western honey-cells; the Sāmans are the honey-makers; the Sāmaveda is the flower; and those are the immortal waters. These very Sāmans heated this Sāmaveda. From it, thus heated, there was produced as its essence glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. That flowed out and took refuge around the sun; that indeed is this dark form of the sun.
Thus ends the third section.

Now, those rays of his that point northward are his northern honey-cells; the Atharvans and Aṅgirases are the honey-makers; the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are the flower; and those are the immortal waters. These very Atharvans and Aṅgirases heated this Itihāsa and Purāṇa. From it, thus heated, there arose as its essence glory, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. That flowed forth; it took refuge around the sun. That indeed is this very dark form of the sun which appears beyond [the other colors].
Thus ends the fourth section.

Now, those rays of his that point upward are his upward honey-cells; the secret instructions are the honey-makers; Brahman is the flower; and they are the immortal waters. These very secret instructions heated that Brahman. From it, thus heated, there was produced as its essence (rasa) fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. That flowed forth; it took refuge all around the sun. That is indeed this which appears as if shimmering in the middle of the sun. These, indeed, are the essences of essences. For the Vedas are essences, and these are their essences. These, indeed, are the immortals of immortals. For the Vedas are immortal, and these are their immortals.
Thus ends the fifth section.

Now, that which is the first nectar, the Vasus subsist upon it with Agni as their mouth. Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by seeing this nectar. (3.6.1) They enter into this very form and emerge from this very form. He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Vasus themselves, is satisfied merely by seeing this nectar with Agni as his mouth. He enters into this very form and emerges from this very form. (3.6.2)
As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, for that long he attains the lordship and sovereignty of the Vasus.
Thus ends the sixth section.

Now, as for the second nectar, the Rudras subsist upon it with Indra as their mouth. Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar. (3.7.1) They enter into this very form, and from this form they emerge. (3.7.2) He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Rudras themselves, is satisfied by beholding this very nectar with Indra as his mouth. He enters into this very form, and from this form he emerges. (3.7.3) As long as the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, twice that long does it rise in the south and set in the north; for so long does he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Rudras. (3.7.4)
Thus ends the seventh section.

Now, as for that third nectar, the Ādityas subsist upon it with Varuṇa as their mouth. Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar. (3.8.1) They enter into this very form, and from this form they emerge. (3.8.2) He who thus knows this nectar becomes one of the Ādityas themselves; with Varuṇa as his mouth, he is satisfied by beholding this very nectar. He enters into this very form, and from this form he emerges. (3.8.3) As long as the sun rises in the south and sets in the north, twice as long does it rise in the west and set in the east; for so long he attains the sovereignty and self-rule of the Ādityas. (3.8.4)
Thus ends the eighth section.

Now, as for that fourth nectar, the Maruts subsist upon it with Soma as their mouth. Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this nectar. (3.9.1) They enter into this very form, and from this form they emerge. (3.9.2) He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Maruts themselves, is satisfied merely by beholding this nectar with Soma as his mouth. He enters into this very form, and from this form he emerges. (3.9.3) As long as the sun rises in the west and sets in the east, twice as long does it rise in the north and set in the south; for so long does he attain the sovereignty and self-rule of the Maruts. (3.9.4)
Thus ends the ninth section.

Now, as for that fifth nectar, upon it the Sādhyas subsist with Brahmā as their mouth. Truly, the gods neither eat nor drink; they are satisfied merely by beholding this very nectar. (3.10.1) They enter into this very form and emerge from this very form. He who knows this nectar thus, becoming one of the Sādhyas themselves, is satisfied by beholding this very nectar through the mouth of Brahmā. He enters into this very form and emerges from this very form. (3.10.2–3) As long as the sun rises in the north and sets in the south, twice as long does he rise above and set below; for so long he attains the overlordship and sovereignty of the Sādhyas. (3.10.4)
Thus ends the tenth section.
Then, having risen above that, he neither rises nor sets; he stands alone in the middle. Regarding this, there is this verse: 3.11.1.
"Truly, there it never sets nor ever rises;
by that truth, O Brahman, may I not be harmed. || 3.11.2 ||

"Verily, for him neither does the sun rise nor does it set; for him there is only one continuous day, he who knows this secret doctrine (*brahmopaniṣad*) of Brahman in this way. (3.11.3) Brahmā told this to Prajāpati; Prajāpati told it to Manu; and Manu told it to his offspring. This very same Brahman-father told this Brahman to his eldest son, Uddālaka Āruṇi. (3.11.4) A father should indeed impart this Brahman only to his eldest son or to a worthy disciple; never to anyone else whatsoever. Even if someone were to give him this entire earth, surrounded by water and filled with wealth, this [knowledge] is far more than that. (3.11.5–6)
Thus ends the eleventh section.
The Gāyatrī indeed is this entire world, whatever exists here. The Gāyatrī is speech; for speech sings (gāyati) and protects (trāyate) this entire world. 3.12.1.

That which is Gāyatrī is indeed this very earth; for upon it all that exists is established, and nothing transcends it. (3.12.2) That which is the earth is indeed this body within the person here; for in it these vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are established, and they do not transcend it. (3.12.3) That which is the body within the person is indeed this heart within the person here; for in it these vital breaths are established, and they do not transcend it. (3.12.4) This is that Gāyatrī, which has four feet and is sixfold. This same fact is declared by a *ṛc* verse: (3.12.5)
Such is his greatness, and yet the Puruṣa is even greater than that.
All beings constitute one quarter of him; his three quarters are the immortal in heaven. (3.12.6)

That which is indeed called "Brahman" is this very space that is outside the person. That which is the space outside the person is indeed this space that is within the person. That which is the space within the person is indeed this space that is within the heart. This is full and unchanging. He who knows this obtains full and unchanging prosperity.
Thus ends the twelfth section.

Now, there are indeed five openings for the gods in this heart. That which is its eastern opening is the *prāṇa* (out-breath); that is the eye; that is the sun. One should meditate upon this as "splendor" (*tejas*) and "food-eating" (*annādya*). He who knows this becomes splendid and an eater of food. Now, that which is its southern opening is the *vyāna* (diffused breath); that is the ear; that is the moon. One should meditate upon this as "prosperity" (*śrī*) and "fame" (*yaśas*). He who knows this becomes prosperous and famous. Now, that which is its western opening is the *apāna* (in-breath); that is speech; that is fire. One should meditate upon this as "Vedic luster" (*brahmavarcasa*) and "food-eating. He who knows this becomes possessed of Vedic luster and an eater of food. Now, that which is its northern opening is the *samāna* (equalizing breath); that is the mind; that is Parjanya (the rain-god). One should meditate upon this as "renown" (*kīrti*) and "splendor" (*vyuṣṭi*). He who knows this becomes renowned and splendid. Now, that which is its upward opening is the *udāna* (up-breath); that is the wind; that is space. One should meditate upon this as "vital force" (*ojas*) and "greatness" (*maha*). He who knows this becomes possessed of vital force and greatness.

These five persons of Brahman are indeed the gatekeepers of the heavenly world. He who knows these five persons of Brahman as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world has a hero born in his family; he attains the heavenly world, he who knows these five persons of Brahman as the gatekeepers of the heavenly world. 3.13.6.

Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the highest worlds above all others—that is indeed this very light which is within this person here. This is its perception: when one perceives warmth by touch in this body. This is its hearing: when, having closed one's ears, one hears as it were a rumbling, as it were a thundering, as it were the crackling of a blazing fire. One should meditate upon this as "the seen and the heard. He who knows this becomes beautiful of form and famous—yes, he who knows this, he who knows this.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

"Indeed, all this is Brahman, born from it, dissolved in it, and breathing in it; one should meditate on it with a calm mind. Now, a person consists of volition (*kratu*); according to his volition in this world, so does a person become after departing from here. He should therefore form a volition. 3.14.1.

Consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body, whose form is light, whose resolve is true, whose nature is space, performing all actions, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, he has pervaded all this; he is without speech and without concern. 3.14.2 This is my Self within the heart, smaller than a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a mustard seed, or a grain of millet, or the kernel of a grain of millet. This is my Self within the heart, greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate region, greater than the sky, greater than these worlds.

He who possesses all works, all desires, all odors, and all tastes; who has reached this entire world, who is speechless and indifferent—this is my Self within the heart. This is Brahman. "Upon departing from here, I shall attain Him"—he who has such a conviction truly has no doubt. Thus indeed said Śāṇḍilya, yes, Śāṇḍilya. 3.14.4.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.
The treasury has the intermediate space for its belly and the earth for its base; it does not decay.
The quarters are its corners and the sky is its upper opening.
This is that treasury, the container of wealth; upon it all this universe is supported.

Of that [cow], the eastern direction is named Juhū; the southern is named Sahamānā; the western is named Rājñī; the northern is named Subhūtā. Vāyu is their calf. He who knows this Vāyu as the calf of the directions does not weep for the loss of a son. I know this Vāyu as the calf of the directions; may I not weep for the loss of a son. 3.15.2.
I take refuge in the inviolable treasury with this, with this, with this;
I take refuge in the vital breath with this, with this, with this; I take refuge in Bhūḥ with this, with this, with this;
I take refuge in Bhuvaḥ with this, with this, with this; I take refuge in Svaḥ with this, with this, with this.
When I said, "I take refuge in Prāṇa," Prāṇa indeed is all this being that exists here as anything whatsoever; it was to that very thing that you then resorted. 3.15.4.
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in Bhūḥ," I thereby said, "I take refuge in the earth, I take refuge in the intermediate space, I take refuge in heaven. 3.15.5.
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in Bhuvas," I meant: "I take refuge in Agni, I take refuge in Vāyu, I take refuge in Āditya. Thus did I speak. 3.15.6.
Now, as for what I said, "I take refuge in *svaḥ*," I meant: "I take refuge in the Ṛgveda; I take refuge in the Yajurveda; I take refuge in the Sāmaveda. Thus indeed did I speak. 3.15.7.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.

Man, indeed, is the sacrifice. Those twenty-four years of his constitute the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*). The *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables, and the morning libation belongs to the *gāyatrī*. The Vasus are connected with this part of him. The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the Vasus, for they cause all this to abide. If anything should afflict him during that stage of life, he should say: "O Vasus, the vital breaths! Extend this morning libation of mine to the midday libation, so that the sacrifice may not be lost in the midst of the vital breaths, the Vasus. Thereupon he rises up from it and becomes free from disease.

Now, those forty-four years constitute the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*). The *triṣṭubh* meter consists of forty-four syllables; the midday libation belongs to the *triṣṭubh*. The Rudras are dependent upon it. The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the Rudras, for they cause all this to weep (*rodayanti*). If anything should afflict him during that period of life, he should say: "O vital breaths, O Rudras, extend this midday libation of mine to the third libation, so that the sacrifice may not be lost in the midst of the vital breaths, the Rudras! Thereupon he rises up from it and becomes free from disease.

Now, those forty-eight years constitute the third pressing. The *jagatī* meter consists of forty-eight syllables; the third pressing belongs to the *jagatī*. The Ādityas are connected with this [third pressing]. The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the Ādityas, for they take up all this [world]. If anything should afflict him during that period of life, he should say: "O vital breaths, O Ādityas, extend this third pressing of mine along with my life-force, so that I, the sacrifice, may not perish in the midst of the vital breaths and the Ādityas! He rises from that [affliction] and becomes free from disease.

Knowing this, Mahidāsa Aitareya indeed said: "Why do you afflict me with this, I who shall not depart because of it? He lived for one hundred and sixteen years. One who knows this lives for one hundred and sixteen years. 3.16.7.
Thus ends the sixteenth section.

When he feels hunger, when he feels thirst, and when he does not find delight—these are his *dīkṣā*s (initiatory consecrations). (3.17.1) Then, when he eats, when he drinks, and when he finds delight—that is how he proceeds with the *upasad* rites. (3.17.2) Then, when he laughs, when he eats solid food, and when he engages in sexual intercourse—that is how he proceeds with the *stotra* and *śastra* hymns. (3.17.3) Then, austerity, charity, uprightness, non-violence, and truthfulness—these are his *dakṣiṇā*s (sacrificial fees). (3.17.4)
Therefore they say, "He will procreate; he has procreated. That is merely his rebirth; death itself is the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).

Ghora Āṅgirasa, having taught this to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, said: "He indeed became free from thirst. At the time of his end, he should take recourse to these three [mantras]: 'Thou art the imperishable; thou art the unswerving; thou art sharpened by the vital breath. In this regard, there are these two ṛg-verses. (3.17.6)
From the beginning, from the ancient seed; we, beholding the light higher than darkness,
behold the sun, the god among the gods, the higher light, the heaven.
"We have gone to the highest light"—thus [he says], "the highest light. 3.17.7.
Thus ends the seventeenth section.

"One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman"—this is with respect to the self (ādhyātmam). Now, with respect to the divine (adhidaivatam): "Space is Brahman. Thus both have been taught: that which pertains to the self and that which pertains to the divine. 3.18.1.

This Brahman has four quarters: speech is one quarter, breath is one quarter, the eye is one quarter, and the ear is one quarter; thus with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). Now, with respect to the divine (*adhidaivata*): fire is one quarter, wind is one quarter, the sun is one quarter, and the quarters of space are one quarter; thus both are taught—both with respect to the self and with respect to the divine. (3.18.2)
Speech indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman. It shines and glows with fire as its light. He who knows this shines and glows with fame, renown, and the splendor of sacred knowledge. 3.18.3.

Breath alone is the fourth foot of Brahman. It shines and glows with Vāyu as its light. He who knows this shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa). 3.18.4.

The eye indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman. It shines and glows with the sun as its light. He who knows this shines and glows with fame, with glory, and with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). 3.18.5.

The ear indeed is the fourth foot of Brahman. It shines and glows with the quarters as its light. He who knows this shines and glows with fame, renown, and the splendor of sacred knowledge—yea, he who knows this. 3.18.6.
Thus ends the eighteenth section.

"Āditya is Brahman"—this is the instruction. Its further explanation follows: In the beginning, this world was indeed non-existent; it became existent; it developed. It turned into an egg. It lay for the duration of a year. It split open. Those two halves of the eggshell became silver and gold. (3.19.1) That which was silver is this earth; that which was gold is the sky; what was the outer membrane is the mountains; what was the inner membrane is the mist together with the clouds; what were the veins are the rivers; and the water contained within is the ocean. (3.19.2) Then, that which was born there is yonder Āditya. As he was being born, shouts and cries of joy arose after him, as did all beings and all desires. Therefore, at his rising and at his setting, shouts and cries of joy arise after him, as do all beings and all desires. (3.19.3)
He who, knowing it thus, venerates this Āditya as Brahman—for him, indeed, virtuous sounds will quickly come to him and will repeatedly resound around him, yes, they will repeatedly resound. 3.19.4.
Thus ends the nineteenth section.
Thus ends the third chapter.
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was a man of faith, a giver of much, a provider of many meals, and one who maintained dwellings on all sides, thinking, "People shall eat my food from every direction. (4.1.1)

Then, indeed, some swans flew by at night. One swan addressed another thus: "Ho there, O Bhallākṣa, Bhallākṣa! The light of Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa is spread out as far as the sky; do not touch it, lest it consume you. The other replied to him: "Who is this person you speak of, who is like Raikva with his cart? [The first asked: "But how is Raikva with his cart? [The other replied: "He who... 4.1.3.

Just as when one has won a prize in a game of dice, all the lower stakes are gathered together, even so everything that people do that is good converges upon him who knows what he knows—this which I have told you. 4.1.4.
Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa overheard this. As he was rising, he said to his charioteer, "My dear man, have you spoken of Raikva as if he were Sayugvā? For who indeed is this Sayugvā Raikva? 4.1.5.

Just as when one has won a prize in a game of dice, all the lower stakes are gathered together toward him, even so everything that people do that is good converges upon him who knows what he [the teacher] knows—“He who knows that which he knows, has been told this by me. 4.1.6.
Thus ends the first section.

Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking six hundred cows, a gold necklace, and a chariot drawn by mules, approached him. He said to him: "O Raikva, here are six hundred cows, this gold necklace, and this chariot drawn by mules. Teach me, O venerable sir, that deity whom you worship. The other replied to him: "Ha! O Śūdra, let these remain with you along with the cows! Then Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, taking a thousand cows, a gold necklace, a chariot drawn by mules, and his daughter, approached him again. He said to him: "O Raikva, here are a thousand cows, this gold necklace, this chariot drawn by mules, this wife, and this village in which you dwell. Teach me, O venerable sir."

As he was lifting her face toward him, he said, "I have taken these [cows] away from you; you would have made me speak with this mouth of a Śūdra! These are the Raikvaparṇas by name among the Mahāvṛṣas, where he dwelt with him. To him, he spoke. 4.2.5.
Thus ends the second section.

Air, indeed, is the absorber. When fire goes out, it passes into air; when the sun sets, it passes into air; when the moon sets, it passes into air. When the waters dry up, they pass into air. For air absorbs all these. This is with respect to the deities.

Now, with respect to the self: breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the absorber (*saṃvarga*). When one sleeps, speech merges into breath, sight merges into breath, hearing merges into breath, and the mind merges into breath; for breath indeed absorbs all these. 4.3.3.

These two, indeed, are the two absorbers: Vāyu among the gods and Prāṇa among the vital breaths. Now, while Śaunaka Kāpeya and Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni were being served food, a religious student begged of them. They both did not give to him. He said:
“The one great-souled god has swallowed the four; who is he, the guardian of the world?
O Kāpeya, mortals do not perceive him, O Abhipratārin, though he dwells in many forms.”
"Because this food was not given to him for whom it was intended," so [they say]. || 4.3.6 ||
Reflecting upon this, Śaunaka Kāpeya returned [to his teacher] with the following verses:
"The Self of the gods, the progenitor of creatures, with golden tusks, the consumer, the wise one—
his greatness they call vast, since, being himself uneaten, he eats that which is not food."
"O student, it is indeed thus that we do not worship this; give him alms," [they say]. 4.3.7.

They indeed gave it to him. These five and those other five, being ten, constitute the *kṛta* throw. Therefore, in all directions, food itself is the *daśakṛta*. This is that Virāj, the eater of food. By her, this whole world is seen. He who knows thus—this whole world becomes seen by him, and he becomes an eater of food; he who knows thus, he who knows thus. 4.3.8.
Thus ends the third section.

Satyakāma Jābāla addressed his mother Jābālā: "I wish to live the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*). Of what lineage (*gotra*) am I? (4.4.1) She said to him: "I do not know this, my son—of what lineage you are. In my youth, while I was serving many people, I obtained you. Therefore, I do not know of what lineage you are. I am Jābālā by name; you are Satyakāma by name. You should simply say, 'Satyakāma Jābāla. (4.4.2)

He went to Hāridrumata Gautama and said, "I shall live the life of a religious student under your lordship; let me approach your lordship. He said to him, "Of what lineage are you, my dear? He replied, "I do not know this, sir, of what lineage I am. I asked my mother, and she answered me: 'In my youth, while I was wandering about much as a servant, I conceived you. Therefore, I do not know of what lineage you are. I am Jabālā by name, and you are Satyakāma by name. Thus, sir, I am Satyakāma Jābāla."

He said to him: "It is not right for one who is not a Brahmin to speak thus. Bring fuel, my dear; I will initiate you. You have not departed from the truth. Having initiated him, he set aside four hundred lean and weak cows and said: "Follow these, my dear. As he was driving them away, he said: "I shall not return until they have become a thousand. He lived abroad for many years, and when they had become a thousand—4.4.5.
Thus ends the fourth section.
Then a bull addressed him, saying, "Satyakāma! He replied, "Yes, venerable sir. "We have completed our thousand, my dear; take us to the teacher's house. 4.5.1.

"And I shall tell you one quarter of Brahman. "Let the Blessed One tell it to me," [he said]. He said to him: "The eastern direction is one part (kalā); the western direction is one part; the southern direction is one part; the northern direction is one part. This, my dear, is the four-part quarter of Brahman named 'The Radiant' (prakāśavān). 4.5.2.

He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Radiant," becomes radiant in this world; he wins radiant worlds—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "The Radiant. 4.5.3.
Thus ends the fifth section.

"Agni will tell you one quarter," he said. On the following day, he drove the cows forward. When they had gathered in the evening, he built up a fire there, penned the cows, added fuel, and sat down behind the fire facing the east. 4.6.1.

Agni spoke to him, saying, "Satyakāma! He replied, "Revered sir. "Dear boy, let me tell you one quarter of Brahman," he said. "Let my revered sir tell me," he replied. To him he then said: "The earth is one part; the intermediate space is one part; the sky is one part; the ocean is one part. This, dear boy, is the four-part quarter of Brahman named 'the Endless' (Anantavān). He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part quarter of Brahman as 'the Endless,' becomes endless in this world. He wins endless worlds who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part quarter of Brahman as 'the Endless.'
Thus ends the sixth section.

"Haṃsa will tell you the foot," he said. On the following day, he drove the cows toward home. When they had gathered in the evening, he built a fire, penned the cows, added fuel, and sat down to the west of the fire, facing east. 4.7.1.

A swan, having approached him, said, "Satyakāma! He replied, "Revered sir. "Dear boy, let me tell you one quarter of Brahman," [the swan] said. "Let the revered sir tell me," [Satyakāma] replied. To him he spoke: "Fire is a quarter; the sun is a quarter; the moon is a quarter; lightning is a quarter. This, dear boy, is the four-quartered quarter of Brahman called 'The Luminous' (Jyotiṣmat). He who, knowing it thus, venerates this four-quartered quarter of Brahman as "The Luminous," becomes luminous in this world. He wins luminous worlds, he who, knowing it thus, venerates this four-quartered quarter of Brahman as "The Luminous."
Thus ends the seventh section.

"Madgu will tell you the foot," he said. On the following day, he drove the cows toward home. When they had gathered together at evening, he built up a fire, penned the cows, added fuel, and sat down behind the fire, facing the east. 4.8.1.
A water-crow, flying down toward him, called out, "Satyakāma! He replied, "Revered sir. 4.8.2.

"Dear boy, let me tell you one quarter of Brahman. "Let the venerable sir tell it to me. He said to him: "Breath is a quarter; sight is a quarter; hearing is a quarter; mind is a quarter. This, dear boy, is the four-quartered quarter of Brahman named 'Possessing a Foundation'. 4.8.3.

He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "possessing an abode," becomes possessed of an abode in this world; he wins worlds that possess an abode—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon this four-part foot of Brahman as "possessing an abode. 4.8.4.
Thus ends the eighth section.

He arrived at the teacher’s house. The teacher addressed him, saying, “Satyakāma! He replied, “Revered sir. “You shine, my dear, like one who knows Brahman. Who has instructed you? “Other than human beings,” he replied. “But may your reverence yourself tell it to me, as you wish. “For I have heard from those like your reverence that knowledge, when learned from a teacher, reaches its highest fulfillment. To him he taught this very thing. Regarding this, it is said: “In this matter, nothing whatsoever is omitted—nothing whatsoever is omitted.”
Thus ends the ninth section.

Upakosala Kāmalāyana lived as a religious student with Satyakāma Jābāla. For twelve years he tended his fires. While he was doing so, he allowed other students to return home after completing their studies, yet he did not allow him to return. His wife said to him, "This student has performed his penance and has served the fires well. Let the fires not speak out against you; please grant him leave. But even without granting him leave, the teacher went away on a journey. 4.10.1–2

He resolved not to eat because of illness. His teacher’s wife said to him, “Student, eat! Why do you not eat? He replied, “There are many desires here in this person, each with its own course. I am filled with diseases; I will not eat. Then the fires deliberated among themselves: “The student has been devoted to us; he has served us well. Come, let us speak to him. They said to him, “Breath is Brahman; *ka* is Brahman; *kha* is Brahman. He said, “I understand that breath is Brahman, but I do not understand *ka* and *kha*. They said, “That which is indeed *ka* is *kha*; that which is *kha* is *ka*. Thus they spoke to him of both breath and space.
Thus ends the tenth section.

Then the Gārhapatya fire instructed him: "The earth, fire, and food—these are Āditya. That person who is seen in Āditya, he am I; he indeed am I. He who, knowing this thus, meditates upon him, shakes off evil-doing. He becomes a possessor of the world; he reaches a full lifespan; he lives radiantly. His descendants do not perish. We attend upon him and enjoy him both in this world and in the yonder world—he who, knowing this thus, meditates upon him.
Thus ends the eleventh section.

Then the Anvāhāryapacana fire instructed him: "The waters, the quarters, the stars, and the moon—this person who is seen in the moon, that am I; he indeed am I. He who, knowing this, meditates upon him thus, shakes off evil-doing. He becomes a possessor of the world, reaches a full lifespan, and lives radiantly. His descendants do not perish. We serve him and enjoy his bounty both in this world and in the yonder world—whoever, knowing this, meditates upon him thus.
Thus ends the twelfth section.

Then the Āhavanīya fire instructed him: "Breath, space, heaven, lightning—this person who is seen in the lightning, that am I; that very one am I. He who, knowing it thus, worships it, destroys his evil deeds, becomes a possessor of the world, reaches a full lifespan, and lives radiantly. His descendants do not perish. We serve him and enjoy him both in this world and in the yonder world—whoever, knowing it thus, worships it.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

They said, "Upakosala, my dear, this is our knowledge of the Self; but your teacher will tell you the way. Then his teacher arrived. The teacher addressed him, saying, "Upakosala! He replied, "Revered sir. "The face of one who knows Brahman, my dear, shines as it were. Who has instructed you? "Who would dare instruct me, sir? he said, while feigning concealment. "Surely these fires here are such [teachers], yet they are different," he said, pointing toward the sacrificial fires. "What, then, my dear, did they say to you? "They spoke of the worlds, indeed, my dear," he replied. "But I shall tell you that, so that evil action does not cling to one who knows thus—just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf. Let the venerable sir speak to me. He then spoke to him.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

"This person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self," he said. "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. Even if one pours clarified butter or water into it, it flows away along the eyelashes. 4.15.1.
They call this "the gathering of all that is desirable" (*saṃyadvāma*), for indeed, all desirable things gather toward it. All desirable things gather toward him who knows this. 4.15.2.

He is indeed Vāmanī (the Bringer of Wealth). For he leads all things that are desirable. He who knows this leads all things that are desirable. 4.15.3 He is indeed Bhāmanī (the Shining One). For he shines in all worlds. He who knows this shines in all worlds. 4.15.4

Now, whether they perform the funeral rites for him here or not, they all surely pass into the flame; from the flame into the day; from the day into the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight into those six months during which the sun moves northward; from those months into the year; from the year into the sun; from the sun into the moon; from the moon into the lightning. There is a person who is non-human (*amānava*); he leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods, the path to Brahman. Those who set out upon it do not return to this human whirlpool—they do not return. 4.15.5
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
This indeed is the sacrifice that blows here; for as it blows, it purifies all this. Since it purifies all this as it blows, therefore it is the sacrifice. Its two paths are mind and speech. 4.16.1.

Of these two, the Brahman prepares one with his mind, while the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, and the Udgātṛ prepare the other with their speech. When, after the Prātaranuvāka has been commenced but before the Paridhānīyā verse, the Brahman speaks out [interferes], [the sacrifice is flawed]. 4.16.2.

He prepares only one of the two paths, while the other falls away. Just as a cart traveling on one foot perishes, or a chariot moving with only one wheel comes to ruin, even so does his sacrifice perish. As the sacrifice perishes, the sacrificer perishes along with it; having sacrificed, he becomes worse off. (4.16.3)

Now, when the *prātaranuvāka* has been commenced, if the Brahman does not speak out before the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*), they prepare both tracks; neither one is neglected. Just as a two-footed man walking or a chariot moving on both wheels remains steady, even so his sacrifice remains steady. As the sacrifice remains steady, the sacrificer follows it in remaining steady. Having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous.
Thus ends the sixteenth section.
Prajāpati brooded over the worlds. From them, as they were being brooded upon, he extracted their essences: Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the intermediate space, and Āditya from the sky. 4.17.1.

He brooded over these three deities. From them, as they were being brooded upon, he drew out their essences: from Agni, the Ṛg-verses; from Vāyu, the Yajus-formulas; and from Āditya, the Sāman-chants. (4.17.2)

He brooded over this triple knowledge. From it, as it was being brooded over, he drew out its essences: "Bhūḥ" from the Ṛg-verses, "Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajus-formulas, and "Svaḥ" from the Sāman-chants. (4.17.3)

If, therefore, it should be damaged on account of the *ṛc*, one should offer an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire with the words, "Bhūḥ svāhā! By means of the very essence of the *ṛcs*, by the power of the *ṛcs*, he thereby mends whatever in the sacrifice has been injured on account of the *ṛcs*. || 4.17.4 ||

Now, if it should be damaged on account of the Yajus formulas, one should offer an oblation in the Dakṣiṇāgni with the words, "Bhuvaḥ svāhā! By means of the very essence of the Yajus formulas, by the power of the Yajus formulas, he mends whatever in the sacrifice has been injured on account of the Yajus formulas. || 4.17.5 ||

Now, if it should be damaged on account of the Sāmans, one should offer an oblation in the Āhavanīya fire with the formula, "Svaḥ svāhā! By means of the essence of the Sāmans, by the vigor of the Sāmans, he thereby mends whatever in the sacrifice has been injured on account of the Sāmans. || 4.17.6 ||

Just as one might join gold with salt, silver with gold, tin with silver, lead with tin, iron with lead, wood with iron, and wood with leather—so, by the power of these worlds, of these deities, and of this triple knowledge (trayī-vidyā), he joins together whatever is torn in the sacrifice. Indeed, that sacrifice becomes a "remedy-maker" where there is a Brahman priest who knows thus. That sacrifice indeed inclines toward the north where there is a Brahman priest who knows thus. Of such a Brahman priest who knows thus, there is this traditional verse:
Whithersoever he turns, thither he goes—such is the nature of man.
Let the Brahmin alone act as the officiating priest and protect the Kurus and the horses.

In this way, indeed, such a Brahman protects the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and all the officiating priests. Therefore, one should appoint only such a person as the Brahman, and not one who does not know this, not one who does not know this. 4.17.10.
Thus ends the seventeenth section.
Thus ends the fourth chapter.
Verily, he who knows the oldest and the best becomes indeed the oldest and the best. Breath, indeed, is the oldest and the best. (5.1.1)
He who knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*) indeed becomes the most excellent among his own people. Speech, verily, is the most excellent. 5.1.2.
He who knows the foundation indeed stands firm in this world and in that world; the eye, verily, is the foundation. 5.1.3.
Verily, he who knows attainment—for him desires, both divine and human, are attained. The ear, indeed, is attainment. 5.1.4.
Verily, he who knows the abode becomes the abode of his own people; for the mind, indeed, is the abode. 5.1.5.
