Then, indeed, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) disputed among themselves regarding who was superior, saying, "I am superior! I am superior! They went to their father Prajāpati and said, "Venerable sir, who among us is the best? He said to them, "He among you, upon whose departure the body appears most wretched, he is the best of you."

Speech departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How have you been able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the dumb live—breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind—so [have we lived]. Speech entered back in. The eye departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How have you been able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the blind live—breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, and thinking with the mind—so [have we lived]. The eye entered back in. The ear departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How have you been able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the deaf live—breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and thinking with the mind—so [have we lived]. The ear entered back in. The mind departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How have you been able to live without me? They replied, "Just as children who lack the power of thought live—breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, and hearing with the ear—so [have we lived]. The mind entered back in.

Then the vital breath (*prāṇa*), about to depart, pulled the other vital breaths out, just as a fine horse might tear up the pegs of its foot-tethers. They gathered around him and said, "Venerable sir, remain! You are the best among us; do not depart. Then Speech said to him, "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent one. Then the Eye said to him, "Insofar as I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), you are that foundation. Then the Ear said to him, "Insofar as I am attainment (*saṃpat*), you are that attainment. Then the Mind said to him, "Insofar as I am the abode (*āyatana*), you are that abode. Indeed, they do not call them "Speeches," nor "Eyes," nor "Ears," nor "Minds"; they call them simply "Breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*). For the vital breath indeed becomes all these.
Thus ends the first section.

He said, "What shall be my food? They replied, "Whatever there is here, down to dogs and down to birds. Now, this is indeed the food of breath (*ana*). "Breath" (*ana*) is indeed its manifest name. For one who knows this, nothing whatsoever becomes non-food. He said, "What shall be my clothing? They replied, "Water. Therefore, when they are about to eat, people surround themselves with water both before and after; he indeed becomes a possessor of clothing and remains unclothed (unexposed).
Having told this to Gośruti Vaiyāghrapadya, Satyakāma Jābāla said: "Even if one were to say this to a withered stump, branches would surely grow upon it and leaves would sprout. (5.2.3)

Now, if he should desire to go to the Great [Heaven], having been initiated on the new moon day, on the night of the full moon he should stir a mash of all herbs with curds and honey; then, having offered an oblation of clarified butter into the fire with the words, "To the Eldest, to the Best, svāhā!", he should pour the remnants into the mash. 5.2.4.

Having offered a portion of clarified butter into the fire with the formula, “To Vasiṣṭha, svāhā!”, he should pour the remnants into the mash. Having offered a portion of clarified butter into the fire with the formula, “To the Foundation, svāhā!”, he should pour the remnants into the mash. Having offered a portion of clarified butter into the fire with the formula, “To Success, svāhā!”, he should pour the remnants into the mash. Having offered a portion of clarified butter into the fire with the formula, “To the Abode, svāhā!”, he should pour the remnants into the mash.

Then, having stepped back and placed the stirred offering in his joined palms, he mutters: "Amas by name you are; for all this is indeed yours. He is the eldest, the best, the king, the sovereign lord. May he lead me to the state of being the eldest, the best, the king, and the sovereign lord—may I alone be all this. || 5.2.6 ||
Then, indeed, he sips water line by line with this ṛc:
"We choose that of Savitṛ," with these words he sips; "the food of the god," with these words he sips.
With the words, "The best, the most all-pervading," he sips; with the words, "We meditate upon the swift power of Bhaga," he drinks the whole. || 5.2.7 ||

Having washed the bronze vessel or the wooden cup, he lies down behind the fire on a skin or on the bare ground, restraining his speech and remaining unconquered. If he should see a woman, he should know that the rite has been successful. 5.2.8.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"When, in dreams, one sees a woman during rites performed for the sake of desired objects,
one should recognize prosperity therein— in that vision of a dream, in that vision of a dream."
Thus ends the second section.
Śvetaketu Āruṇeya went to the assembly of the Pañcālas. Pravāhaṇa Jaibali said to him, "Young man, has your father instructed you? "He has, venerable sir," he replied. 5.3.1.

"Do you know where creatures go from here? "No, venerable sir. "Do you know how they return again? "No, venerable sir. "Do you know the point of divergence between the path of the gods and the path of the fathers? "No, venerable sir. (5.3.2)
"Do you know why that world is never filled? "No, venerable sir. "Do you know how, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'? "Not at all, venerable sir. (5.3.3)

"Then, having been instructed by whom did you speak? For how could one who does not know these things claim to have been instructed? He went, dejected, to his father's presence. His father said to him, "The venerable one indeed told me, 'I have instructed you,' even though he had not instructed me. [Gautama said: "A man of the royal class asked me five questions; I was unable to answer even one of them. He (the father) said, "Since you spoke to me thus, it is clear that I do not know even one of these. Had I known them, why would I not have told you? Then Gautama went to the king’s presence. When he arrived, the king offered him the honors due to a guest. In the morning, he came out to meet him. The king said to him, "O venerable Gautama, choose a boon from among human wealth. He replied, "Let human wealth remain yours alone, O King. Tell me that very word which you spoke in the presence of my son. The king became distressed. He (the king) commanded him to stay for a long time. He (Gautama) said to him, "As you have spoken to me, Gautama—since this knowledge has never before gone to the Brāhmaṇas from anyone other than you, therefore, in all the worlds, the governance has belonged only to the Kṣatriya. Then he (the king) spoke to him.
Thus ends the third section.

"Yonder world, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. Of that, the sun is the fuel; the rays are the smoke; the day is the flame; the moon is the embers; and the stars are the sparks. (5.4.1) Into this very fire, the gods offer faith. From that oblation, King Soma comes into being. (5.4.2)
Thus ends the fourth section.

Parjanya, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. Of that, the wind is the fuel; the cloud is the smoke; the lightning is the flame; the thunderbolt is the embers; and the thunderclaps are the sparks. (5.5.1) In this very fire, the gods offer King Soma as an oblation. From that offering, rain comes into being. (5.5.2)
Thus ends the fifth section.

"The earth, indeed, O Gautama, is the fire. Of that, the year is the fuel; space is the smoke; night is the flame; the quarters are the embers; and the intermediate quarters are the sparks. (5.6.1) Into this very fire, the gods offer rain. From that oblation, food comes into being. (5.6.2)
Thus ends the sixth section.

"Man, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. His speech is the fuel; his breath is the smoke; his tongue is the flame; his eye is the embers; his ear is the sparks. (5.7.1) Into this very fire, the gods offer food. From that oblation, semen comes into being. (5.7.2)
Thus ends the seventh section.

"The woman, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. Her lap is the fuel; when he addresses her, that is the smoke; the vulva is the flame; what he performs within is the embers; the orgasms are the sparks. (5.8.1) Into this very fire the gods offer semen; from that oblation, the embryo comes into being. (5.8.2)
Thus ends the eighth section.

"Thus, indeed, in the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man. That embryo, enveloped by the amnion, having lain within for ten or nine months, or for however long, is then born. Once born, he lives as long as his lifespan lasts. When he has passed away and reached his destiny, they carry him from here back to the very fires from which he came and from which he was produced. (5.9.1–2)
Thus ends the ninth section.

Now, those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity—they pass into the light. From the light they go to the day; from the day to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves northward. (5.10.1) From the months they go to the year; from the year to the sun; from the sun to the moon; from the moon to the lightning. There is a person who is not human; he leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods. (5.10.2)

Now, those in this world who worship with the thought, "Sacrifices and meritorious works are a gift," they pass into smoke; from smoke, into night; from night, into the waning half of the month; and from the waning half, into those six months during which the sun moves southward. They do not reach the year. From the months, they go to the world of the fathers; from the world of the fathers, into space; from space, into the moon. That is King Soma, the food of the gods; that is what the gods eat. Having dwelt there until their allotted time is spent, they then return again by the same path as they came—back to space; from space, to the air; having become air, he becomes smoke; having become smoke, he becomes mist; having become mist, he becomes a cloud; having become a cloud, he rains down. They are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans. Indeed, it is more difficult for them to escape from this state. For whoever eats the food and whoever sheds the seed, he becomes that very thing once again.

Therefore, those here whose conduct has been pleasant will, it is likely, attain a pleasant womb—either the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, or the womb of a Kṣatriya, or the womb of a Vaiśya. But those here whose conduct has been foul will, it is likely, attain a foul womb—the womb of a dog, or the womb of a pig, or the womb of a Caṇḍāla. (5.10.7)

Now, those who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small, repeatedly returning creatures, subject to the cycle: "Be born! Die! This is the third station. Because of this, that world is not filled up. Therefore, one should feel aversion toward it. On this point, there is this verse: 5.10.8.1–2. Those who kill Brahmins, who are cruel, who eat what is forbidden, and who drink liquor, go to foul hells after death. Having dwelt there for many years, they are born again in the wombs of dogs, swine, and outcaste dog-cookers. 5.10.8.3–4. Those who have committed minor offenses and are not known to have performed sacrifices go to the womb of a worm, an insect, a bird, a lion, a tiger, a wolf, a hyena, a pig, a donkey, or a camel. Or else, they enter the womb of a dog, a jackal, a vulture, a crow, an owl, or a cormorant. 5.10.8.5–6. Those who have stolen gold, drunk liquor, or killed a Brahmin cannot be purified by any penance; they must remain outside the Vedic fold. But those who have committed other sins can be purified through various rites. 5.10.8.7–8. A man who has stolen gold becomes pure by giving gold; one who has drunk liquor by drinking hot milk; one who has killed a Brahmin by embracing the staff of a student and living in the forest for twelve years, subsisting on alms and eating only once a day at night. 5.10.8.9–10. A woman who has committed such a sin becomes pure by performing the same penances as her husband, or by fasting unto death. One who has associated with such sinners becomes pure by performing the same penances as they, or by fasting unto death. 5.10.8.11–12. One who has stolen grain becomes pure by giving grain; one who has stolen other goods by giving an equal amount of those goods. One who has stolen meat becomes pure by giving meat; one who has stolen sesame seeds by giving sesame seeds. 5.10.8.13–14. One who has stolen clothes becomes pure by giving clothes; one who has stolen a bed by giving a bed; one who has stolen a vehicle by giving a vehicle; one who has stolen fruit by giving fruit. 5.10.8.15–16. One who has stolen water becomes pure by digging a well; one who has stolen fire by giving a fire; one who has stolen a cow by giving a cow; one who has stolen a field by giving a field. 5.10.8.17–18. One who has stolen knowledge becomes pure by teaching it; one who has stolen a wife by giving a wife; one who has stolen a house by giving a house; one who has stolen a village by giving a village. 5.10.8.19–20. One who has stolen a kingdom becomes pure by giving a kingdom; one who has stolen a horse by giving a horse; one who has stolen a woman by giving a woman; one who has stolen a slave by giving a slave. 5.10.8.21–22. One who has stolen a gem becomes pure by giving a gem; one who has stolen a pearl by giving a pearl; one who has stolen a conch by giving a conch; one who has stolen a coral by giving a coral. 5.10.8.23–24. One who has stolen a diamond becomes pure by giving a diamond; one who has stolen a ruby by giving a ruby; one who has stolen a lapis lazuli by giving a lapis lazuli; one who has stolen a crystal by giving a crystal. 5.10.8.25–26. One who has stolen a pearl shell becomes pure by giving a pearl shell; one who has stolen a shell by giving a shell; one who has stolen a tortoise by giving a tortoise; one who has stolen a fish by giving a fish. 5.10.8.27–28. One who has stolen a deer becomes pure by giving a deer; one who has stolen a bird by giving a bird; one who has stolen a goat by giving a goat; one who has stolen a sheep by giving a sheep. 5.10.8.29–30. One who has stolen a horse becomes pure by giving a horse; one who has stolen a chariot by giving a chariot; one who has stolen a weapon by giving a weapon; one who has stolen a tool by giving a tool. 5.10.8.31–32. One who has stolen a book becomes pure by giving a book; one who has stolen a manuscript by giving a manuscript; one who has stolen a scroll by giving a scroll; one who has stolen a tablet by giving a tablet. 5.10.8.33–34. One who has stolen a seat becomes pure by giving a seat; one who has stolen a mat by giving a mat; one who has stolen a rug by giving a rug; one who has stolen a blanket by giving a blanket. 5.10.8.35–36. One who has stolen a garment becomes pure by giving a garment; one who has stolen a turban by giving a turban; one who has stolen a head-dress by giving a head-dress; one who has stolen an ornament by giving an ornament. 5.10.8.37–38. One who has stolen a ring becomes pure by giving a ring; one who has stolen a bracelet by giving a bracelet; one who has stolen an earring by giving an earring; one who has stolen a necklace by giving a necklace. 5.10.8.39–40. One who has stolen a garland becomes pure by giving a garland; one who has stolen a flower by giving a flower; one who has stolen a scent by giving a scent; one who has stolen a perfume by giving a perfume. 5.10.8.41–42. One who has stolen a medicine becomes pure by giving a medicine; one who has stolen a potion by giving a potion; one who has stolen a food by giving a food; one who has stolen a drink by giving a drink. 5.10.8.43–44. One who has stolen a vegetable becomes pure by giving a vegetable; one who has stolen a fruit by giving a fruit; one who has stolen a root by giving a root; one who has stolen a leaf by giving a leaf. 5.10.8.45–46. One who has stolen a grass becomes pure by giving a grass; one who has stolen a wood by giving a wood; one who has stolen a stone by giving a stone; one who has stolen a clay by giving a clay. 5.10.8.47–48. One who has stolen a water-basin becomes pure by giving a water-basin; one who has stolen a well by giving a well; one who has stolen a tank by giving a tank; one who has stolen a pond by giving a pond. 5.10.8.49–50. One who has stolen a river becomes pure by building a bridge; one who has stolen a mountain by giving a mountain; one who has stolen a forest by giving a forest; one who has stolen a grove by giving a grove. 5.10.8.51–52. One who has stolen a city becomes pure by giving a city; one who has stolen a town by giving a town; one who has stolen a district by giving a district; one who has stolen a country by giving a country. 5.10.8.53–54. One who has stolen a world becomes pure by giving a world; one who has stolen a heaven by giving a heaven; one who has stolen a liberation by giving a liberation; one who has stolen a truth by giving a truth. 5.10.8.55–56. One who has stolen a dharma becomes pure by giving a dharma; one who has stolen a virtue by giving a virtue; one who has stolen a merit by giving a merit; one who has stolen a good by giving a good. 5.10.8.57–58. One who has stolen a blessing becomes pure by giving a blessing; one who has stolen a fortune by giving a fortune; one who has stolen a prosperity by giving a prosperity; one who has stolen a glory by giving a glory. 5.10.8.59–60. One who has stolen a fame becomes pure by giving a fame; one who has stolen a reputation by giving a reputation; one who has stolen a honor by giving an honor; one who has stolen a respect by giving a respect. 5.10.8.61–62. One who has stolen a love becomes pure by giving a love; one who has stolen a friendship by giving a friendship; one who has stolen a devotion by giving a devotion; one who has stolen a faith by giving a faith. 5.10.8.63–64. One who has stolen a hope becomes pure by giving a hope; one who has stolen a desire by giving a desire
A thief of gold, one who drinks liquor, one who violates the bed of his guru, and a killer of a Brahmin—these four fall, as does the fifth who associates with them. (5.10.9)

Now, indeed, he who knows these five fires in this way is not tainted by evil even while associating with those [who are evil]. He becomes pure, cleansed, and possesses a world of merit—he who knows thus, he who knows thus. 5.10.10.
Thus ends the tenth section.

Prācīnaśāla Aupamanyava, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, Jana Śārkarākṣya, and Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi—these great householders and great Vedic scholars, having come together, engaged in a philosophical inquiry: "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? (5.11.1)
They came to an agreement: "Venerable sirs, this Uddālaka Āruṇi is currently studying this very Self as Vaiśvānara; let us go to him. So they went to him. 5.11.2.

He reflected: "These great householders and great Vedic scholars will question me; I may not be able to answer everything to them. Come now, I shall instruct another. He said to them: "Venerable sirs, this Aśvapati, the King of Kekaya, is currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self. Come, let us go to him. So they went to him.
When they had arrived, he caused separate honors to be prepared for each of them. Rising early in the morning, he said:
"In my realm there is no thief, no miser, no drunkard;
no one who has not established the sacred fires, no one who is ignorant, and no one who acts wantonly—how then could there be a wanton woman?"

"Venerable sirs, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice. As much wealth as I shall give to each individual officiating priest, so much shall I give to your venerable selves. May the venerable sirs dwell [here]. 5.11.5.
They said: "Whatever purpose a person may pursue, one should speak to him regarding that very thing. You are currently studying this Vaiśvānara Self; tell us about that very Self. 5.11.6.
He said to them, "I shall answer you in the morning. With fuel in their hands, they returned to him in the forenoon. Without having initiated them, he spoke this to them. || 5.11.7 ||
Thus ends the eleventh section.

"Aupamanyava, upon which self do you meditate? "On the sky alone, O venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is the Vaiśvānara Self, the one with beautiful light (Sutejas), which you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, Soma is seen being pressed, poured out, and offered in your lineage. "You eat food; you see what is dear. He who meditates on this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there is spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) in his lineage. However, this is only the head of the Self," he said. "Your head would have fallen off had you not come to me."
Thus ends the twelfth section.

Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi: "Prācīnayogya, upon which Self do you meditate? "Upon Āditya alone, O venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is the Self Vaiśvānara of all forms, whom you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, many things of all forms are seen in your family: a chariot drawn by mules, female slaves, and gold neck-ornaments. You eat food and see what is dear; he who meditates on this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food and sees what is dear, and there is spiritual luster in his family. But this is only the eye of the Self," he said. "You would have become blind had you not come to me."
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: "O Vaiyāghrapadya, upon which Self do you meditate? "Upon Vāyu alone, O venerable King," he replied. "This is indeed the Self called Vaiśvānara, whose paths are manifold (pṛthagvartman), whom you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, offerings come to you from various directions, and rows of chariots follow you in various directions. "You eat food; you see what is dear. He who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) in his family. But this [Vāyu] is only the breath of the Self," he said. "Your breath would have departed had you not come to me."
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

Then he said to Jana Śārkarākṣya: "Śārkarākṣya, upon which Self do you meditate? "Space alone, O Venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is the manifold Self, Vaiśvānara, whom you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, you are manifold in offspring and in wealth. You eat food and see what is dear. He who meditates on this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food, sees what is dear, and there is spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) in his family. But this is only the trunk of the Self," he said. "Your trunk would have perished had you not come to me."
Thus ends the fifteenth section.

Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: "O Vaiyāghrapadya, upon which Self do you meditate? "Water alone, O venerable King," he replied. "This indeed is the Rayi (wealth) Self, the Vaiśvānara, which you meditate upon as the Self. Therefore, you are wealthy and prosperous. "You eat food and see what is dear. He who meditates thus upon this Vaiśvānara Self eats food, sees what is dear, and there arises spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family. "But this is only the bladder of the Self," he said. "Your bladder would have burst had you not come to me."
Thus ends the sixteenth section.

Then he said to Uddālaka Āruṇi: "Gautama, as what Self do you worship? "Heaven alone, O Venerable King," he replied. "This is indeed the Vaiśvānara Self that is the foundation, which you worship as the Self. Therefore, you are firmly established with offspring and cattle. You eat food and see what is dear; he who worships this Vaiśvānara Self in this way eats food and sees what is dear, and there is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) in his family. But these are only the feet of the Self," he said. "Your feet would have withered away had you not come to me. (5.17.1–2)
Thus ends the seventeenth section.

He said to them: "Indeed, you eat food as if you were each knowing this Vaiśvānara Self separately. But he who meditates upon this Vaiśvānara Self as the measure of a span, as the all-pervading one—he eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves. Now, of this very Vaiśvānara Self, the head is *sutejas* (of brilliant luster), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform), the breath is the self with various paths (*pṛthagvartmātmā*), the trunk is *bahula* (abundant), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), the feet are the earth itself, the chest is the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), the body hair is the sacred grass (*barhis*), the heart is the *gārhapatya* fire, the mind is the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and the mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire.
Thus ends the eighteenth section.

Therefore, whatever food comes first, that is to be offered in sacrifice. When he offers the first oblation, he should offer it with the words, "Svāhā to Prāṇa! Then Prāṇa is satisfied. (5.19.1) When Prāṇa is satisfied, the eye is satisfied; when the eye is satisfied, the sun is satisfied; when the sun is satisfied, the sky is satisfied. When the sky is satisfied, everything whatsoever that the sky and the sun preside over is satisfied. Following its satisfaction, he himself is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge. (5.19.2)
Thus ends the nineteenth section.

Then, that which he should offer as the second oblation, he should offer with: "Svāhā to the diffusive breath (vyāna)! The diffusive breath is satisfied. When the diffusive breath is satisfied, the ear is satisfied. When the ear is satisfied, the moon is satisfied. When the moon is satisfied, the quarters are satisfied. When the quarters are satisfied, whatever is presided over by the quarters and the moon—that is satisfied. Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa).
Thus ends the twentieth section.

Then, that which he should offer as the third, he should offer with: "Svāhā to Apāna! Apāna is satisfied. When Apāna is satisfied, speech is satisfied; when speech is satisfied, Agni is satisfied; when Agni is satisfied, the earth is satisfied; when the earth is satisfied, whatever the earth and Agni preside over is satisfied. Following its satisfaction, he is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*).
Thus ends the twenty-first section.

Then, when one offers the fourth oblation, one should offer it with: "Svāhā to the Common! When the Common is satisfied, the mind is satisfied. When the mind is satisfied, Parjanya is satisfied. When Parjanya is satisfied, lightning is satisfied. When lightning is satisfied, whatever is presided over by both lightning and Parjanya is satisfied. Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge.
Thus ends the twenty-second section.

Then, that which he should offer as the fifth, let him offer with: "Svāhā to the out-breath (udāna)! The out-breath is satisfied. When the out-breath is satisfied, the wind is satisfied; when the wind is satisfied, space is satisfied; when space is satisfied, whatever the wind and space preside over is satisfied. Following its satisfaction, one is satisfied with offspring, cattle, food, splendor, and the luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa).
Thus ends the twenty-third section.

If one who does not know this offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, it would be as if he were to remove the live coals and pour the oblation into ashes. But for one who, knowing it thus, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice, his offering is made in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves.

Just as a tuft of reed-wool thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so are all the evils of one who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice consumed. Therefore, indeed, if one who knows this should give the remains of his food even to a Caṇḍāla, it would be offered by him into Vaiśvānara within his own self. On this there is this verse: 5.24.3–4.1. Just as a tuft of reed-wool thrown into a fire would be consumed, even so are all the evils of one who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra sacrifice consumed. Therefore, indeed, if one who knows this should give the remains of his food even to a Caṇḍāla, it would be offered by him into Vaiśvānara within his own self. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.2. He who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra—whether he gives the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla or to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—it is the same; for he offers it into Vaiśvānara within his own self. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.3. As water on a lotus leaf does not cling, so evil deeds do not cling to one who knows this. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.4. As water on a lotus leaf does not cling, so evil deeds do not cling to one who knows this. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.5. He who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra—whether he gives the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla or to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—it is the same; for he offers it into Vaiśvānara within his own self. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.6. He who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra—whether he gives the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla or to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—it is the same; for he offers it into Vaiśvānara within his own self. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.7. He who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra—whether he gives the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla or to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—it is the same; for he offers it into Vaiśvānara within his own self. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.8. He who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra—whether he gives the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla or to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—it is the same; for he offers it into Vaiśvānara within his own self. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.9. He who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra—whether he gives the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla or to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—it is the same; for he offers it into Vaiśvānara within his own self. On this there is this verse: 5.24.4.10. He who, knowing this thus, offers the Agnihotra—whether he gives the remains of his food to a Caṇḍāla or to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas—it is the same; for he offers it into Vaiśvānara within his own self.
