Just as hungry children here wait upon their mother, so do all beings wait upon the *agnihotra*—they wait upon the *agnihotra*. 5.24.5.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section.

Thus ends the fifth chapter. Śvetaketu, the son of Aruṇi, once lived. His father said to him: "Śvetaketu, live the life of a religious student. Indeed, my dear, no one in our family has ever been unlearned, appearing like a mere kinsman of Brahmins. 6.1.1.

Having approached [his teacher] at twelve years of age, he returned at twenty-four, having studied all the Vedas; being high-minded, considering himself a learned scholar, and arrogant, he went forth. His father said to him: "Śvetaketu, my dear, since you are now so high-minded, considering yourself a learned scholar, and arrogant—did you ask for that instruction by which what is unheard becomes heard, what is unthought becomes thought, and what is unknown becomes known? "How indeed, venerable sir, does that instruction come about?"
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'—so it is. (6.1.4)
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nugget of gold, everything made of gold would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'gold' alone is the reality—so it is. (6.1.5)

"Just as, my dear, by means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of iron might be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while 'iron' alone is the reality—such, my dear, is that instruction. (6.1.6)
"Certainly, those venerable ones did not know this; for had they known it, why would they not have told it to me? Let the venerable one himself tell it to me. "So be it, Soma," he said. 6.1.7.
Thus ends the first section.

"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Regarding this, some say: 'In the beginning this was Non-being alone, one only, without a second; from that Non-being, Being was produced. (6.2.1)

"But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? he said. "How could being be born from non-being? Verily, my dear, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second. It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat. That heat thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted water. Therefore, wherever a person grieves or perspires, water is produced from that very heat. That water thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted food. Therefore, wherever it rains, there food becomes most abundant; for from water alone is food produced."
Thus ends the second section.
Indeed, for these beings, there are exactly three origins: the egg-born, the viviparous, and the soil-born.

That deity thought: "Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms. Let me make each one of them threefold. That deity, having entered these three deities with this very living self, differentiated names and forms; it made each of them threefold. Now, my dear, learn from me how each one of these three deities becomes threefold.
Thus ends the third section.

That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The "fire-ness" of fire has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real. That which is the red form of the sun is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The "sun-ness" of the sun has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real. That which is the red form of the moon is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The "moon-ness" of the moon has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real. That which is the red form of lightning is the form of heat; that which is white is the form of water; that which is black is the form of food. The "lightning-ness" of lightning has departed; it is a mere modification, a verbal handle, a name. Only the three forms are real.

"Indeed, those who knew this in the past—the great householders and the great Vedic scholars—used to say: 'Nothing today shall be uttered by us that has not been heard, thought, or understood. For they had realized this from them. "That which appeared as if red—that they realized was the form of fire (*tejas*). That which appeared as if white—that they realized was the form of water (*āpas*). That which appeared as if black—that they realized was the form of food (*anna*). "And that which appeared as if unknown—that they realized was the combination of these very deities. Now, my dear, learn from me how each of these three deities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold, one after another."
Thus ends the fourth section.

Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts. That which is its coarsest constituent becomes feces; that which is middling becomes flesh; and that which is finest becomes the mind. Water, when drunk, is divided into three parts. That which is its coarsest constituent becomes urine; that which is middling becomes blood; and that which is finest becomes the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Fire, when consumed, is divided into three parts. That which is its coarsest constituent becomes bone; that which is middling becomes marrow; and that which is finest becomes speech. "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said.
Thus ends the fifth section.

"O Somya, when curd is being churned, that subtle essence (*aṇimā*) which rises upward becomes ghee. "In this very same way, O Somya, when food is being eaten, that subtle essence which rises upward becomes the mind (*manas*). "O Somya, when water is being drunk, that subtle essence which rises upward becomes the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "O Somya, when fire is being consumed, that subtle essence which rises upward becomes speech (*vāk*). "For, O Somya, the mind consists of food; the vital breath consists of water; and speech consists of fire. "Venerable sir, please explain this to me further. "So be it, Somya," he said.
Thus ends the sixth section.

“O gentle one, a person consists of sixteen parts. Do not eat for fifteen days; drink water as you wish. Breath is composed of water; it will not be cut off from one who drinks. He did not eat for fifteen days. Then he approached him and said, “Sir, what shall I recite? [The father replied,] “The Ṛg-verses, O gentle one, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants. He said, “They do not come to my mind, sir.”

He said to him: "Just as, my dear, if from a large kindled fire only a single ember the size of a firefly were left, it would not burn much more than that; even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts, only one part remains. With that, you do not now perceive the Vedas. Eat! Then you will understand me. (6.7.3)
He was indeed silent. Then he approached him. Whatever he asked him, he understood it all.

He said to him: "Just as, my dear, if from a large kindled fire a single ember the size of a firefly were left, and one were to kindle it by adding grass to it, it would burn much more than before—even so, my dear, of your sixteen parts, only one part remained. That was kindled when it was nourished with food, and by it you now experience the Vedas. For, my dear, the mind consists of food, the breath consists of water, and speech consists of heat. Then he understood it; yes, he understood it. 6.7.6.
Thus ends the seventh section.

Uddālaka Āruṇi said to his son Śvetaketu: "My dear, learn from me the state of deep sleep. When a person here is said to be 'sleeping,' then, my dear, he has become united with Being (*sat*). He has gone to his own self (*svam apītaḥ*). Therefore they say of him, 'he sleeps' (*svapiti*), for he has gone to his own self. 6.8.1.

"Just as a bird tied by a string, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down upon its very bond; even so, my dear, that mind, having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, settles down upon the vital breath alone. For the mind, my dear, is fastened to the vital breath. 6.8.2

"Understand from me, my dear, hunger and thirst. When a person is said to be 'hungry,' it is the waters that lead away the food he has eaten. Just as one says 'cow-leader,' 'horse-leader,' or 'man-leader,' so they call water 'food-leader' (aśanāya). Now, my dear, understand this sprout that has emerged here: it cannot be without a root. "Where could its root be other than in food? In this very way, my dear, by means of the sprout of food, seek out the root which is water; by means of the sprout of water, my dear, seek out the root which is fire; by means of the sprout of fire, my dear, seek out the root which is Being (sat). All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. (6.8.3–4)

Now, when a person is said to be thirsty, it is the fire (*tejas*) alone that leads the water thus drunk. Just as one speaks of a "leader of cattle," a "leader of horses," or a "leader of men," so does one speak of that fire as "water" (*udanya*). In this matter, my dear, understand that this very thing which has sprouted is a shoot; for it cannot be without a root. (6.8.5) Where could its root be other than in water? My dear, through the shoot of water, seek out the root of fire; my dear, through the shoot of fire, seek out the root of Being (*sat*). My dear, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. Now, my dear, just as each of these three divinities, upon reaching a person, becomes threefold, has already been explained previously. When this person departs, my dear, his speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into fire, and the fire into the highest divinity. (6.8.6)

"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self. That is the Truth. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my son," he said. 6.8.7.
Thus ends the eighth section.

"Just as, my dear, honey-makers collect the juices from trees of various kinds and reduce them to a single unity of juice; and just as those juices do not distinguish there, 'I am the juice of this tree,' or 'I am the juice of that tree'—even so, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know, 'We are merging into Being. Whatever they may be here—a tiger, or a lion, or a wolf, or a boar, or a worm, or a moth, or a gadfly, or a mosquito—that they become, that they enter."

"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self. That is the Truth. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. 6.9.4.
Thus ends the ninth section.

“O dear one, these rivers flow eastward from the east and westward from the west; they go from the ocean to the very ocean and become the ocean itself. Just as they do not know there, ‘I am this one,’ or ‘I am that one,’ even so, my dear, all these creatures, having come from Being, do not know, ‘We are coming from Being. Whatever they may be here—whether a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gadfly, or a mosquito—that they become. (6.10.1–2)

"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self. That is the Truth. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. 6.10.3.
Thus ends the tenth section.

"My dear, if one were to strike this great tree at its root, it would continue to exude sap while living; if one were to strike it in the middle, it would continue to exude sap while living; if one were to strike it at the top, it would continue to exude sap while living. Pervaded by this living self, it stands drinking and rejoicing. (6.11.1) If the living principle leaves one branch of it, then that branch withers. If it leaves a second, then that withers. If it leaves a third, then that withers. When it leaves the whole, the whole withers. (6.11.2)

"In this very way, my dear, understand it," he said. "Verily, this body dies when abandoned by the living self (jīva); the living self does not die. That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; that art thou, Śvetaketu. "Revered sir, please instruct me further," [Śvetaketu said]. "So be it, my dear," he said. (6.11.3)
Thus ends the eleventh section.

"Bring me a fruit from this banyan tree," [he said]. "Here it is, Blessed One. "Break it open. "It is broken open, Blessed One. "What do you see there? "These seeds are as minute as atoms, Blessed One. "My dear, break one of these open. "It is broken open, Blessed One. "What do you see there? "Nothing at all, Blessed One. He said to him: "My dear, that subtle essence which you do not perceive—it is from that very subtle essence, my dear, that this great banyan tree stands. Have faith, my dear!"

"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self. That is the Truth. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. (6.12.3)
Thus ends the twelfth section.

"Place this salt in water, and then come to me in the morning. He did so. He said to him: "My dear, bring that salt which you placed in the water last evening. Having searched for it, he did not find it, for it had completely dissolved. "Well then, taste it from the top," he said. "How is it? "It is salty. "Taste it from the middle. "How is it? "It is salty. "Taste it from the bottom. "How is it? "It is salty. "Having cast it away, then come to me. He did so. It remained there as it was. He said to him: "In truth, my dear, you do not perceive it here; yet, in truth, it is right here."

"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self. That is the Truth. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. 6.13.3.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

"Suppose, my dear, that they were to bring a man from Gandhāra with his eyes bound and then leave him in a desolate place. He might there groan, facing east, north, south, or west, thinking, 'I have been brought here with my eyes bound; I have been left here with my eyes bound. Then, someone might loosen his bonds and tell him, 'Go in this direction; Gandhāra is in that direction. Being wise and intelligent, he would ask his way from village to village and eventually arrive at Gandhāra. In exactly the same way, a person who has a teacher knows: 'For me, there is delay only so long as I am not released; then I shall attain [the goal].'"

"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self. That is the Truth. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. (6.14.3)
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

“O gentle one, when a person is afflicted by illness, his kinsmen sit around him and ask, ‘Do you recognize me? Do you recognize me? As long as his speech has not merged into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity, so long does he recognize them. But when his speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity, then he no longer recognizes them. (6.15.1–2)

"That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self. That is the Truth. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu. "Please, venerable sir, instruct me further. "So be it, my dear," he said. (6.15.3)
Thus ends the fifteenth section.

"O Somya, they bring a man bound by the hand, saying: 'He has stolen; he has committed theft. Heat the axe for him! If he is the doer of that deed, then he makes himself false. Being intent on falsehood, having concealed himself with falsehood, he grasps the heated axe; he is burned, and then he is killed. But if he is not the doer of that deed, then he makes himself true. Being intent on truth, having concealed himself with truth, he grasps the heated axe; he is not burned, and then he is released. (6.16.1–2)

Just as it would not be burned there, so too this whole world has that as its essence. That is the Truth. That is the Self. "That thou art, Śvetaketu. Thus he understood it from him—yes, he understood it. 6.16.3.
Thus ends the sixteenth section.
Thus ends the sixth chapter.

"Teach me, O Venerable One," said Nārada, approaching Sanatkumāra. He said to him, "Approach me with what you already know; thereafter I shall tell you what lies beyond that. He (Nārada) said: *Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.1*

"Venerable sir, I have studied the Rigveda; the Yajurveda; the Samaveda; the Atharvana as the fourth; the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas; the science of ancestral rites; mathematics; the science of portents; the science of treasures; logic; ethics; the science of the gods; the science of sacred knowledge; the science of spirits; the science of politics; the science of the stars; and the science of serpents and celestial beings—this, venerable sir, is what I have studied. (7.1.2)

"Therefore, O Blessed One, I am merely a knower of mantras, not a knower of the Self. For I have heard from those like your reverence that the knower of the Self crosses over sorrow. Thus, O Blessed One, I am in sorrow. May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of this sorrow. He said to him: "Whatever you have studied here, all that is merely name."

It is called the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the Atharvana as the fourth; the Itihasa-Purana as the fifth among the Vedas; the science of the ancestors, the science of the gods, the science of numbers, the science of omens, the science of the Vedic dialogues, the science of the single path, the science of celestial bodies, the science of Brahman, the science of spirits, the science of weapons, the science of the stars, and the science of serpents and divine beings. It is merely a name. Meditate upon Name. (7.1.4)

He who meditates on "Name" as Brahman—so far as Name extends, so far he has unlimited freedom, provided he meditates on "Name" as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than Name? "There is indeed something greater than Name. "May the venerable sir tell me that. 7.1.5.
Thus ends the first section.

Speech is indeed greater than name. Speech makes known the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvaṇa* as the fourth, the *Itihāsa-Purāṇa* as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic, ethics, etymology, the science of the gods, the science of sacred knowledge (*brahmavidyā*), the science of spirits, the science of governance, the science of the stars, the science of serpents and celestial beings; as well as heaven and earth, wind and space, water and fire; gods and humans, cattle and birds, grasses and trees, beasts down to worms, moths, and ants; and both righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant. If speech did not exist, neither righteousness nor unrighteousness would be made known, nor truth nor falsehood, nor the good nor the bad, nor the pleasant nor the unpleasant. It is speech alone that makes all this known. "Meditate upon speech. (7.2.1)

He who meditates on speech as Brahman—so far as speech reaches, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on speech as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than speech? "There is indeed something greater than speech. "May the venerable sir tell that to me. 7.2.2
Thus ends the second section.

The mind, indeed, is greater than speech. Just as one’s fist encompasses two *vāmalaka* fruits, or two jujube berries, or two kola-berries, even so the mind encompasses both speech and name. When one intends with the mind, "I would study the sacred hymns," then one studies them; "I would perform rituals," then one performs them; "I would desire sons and cattle," then one desires them; "I would desire this world and the other world," then one desires them. For the mind is the self; the mind is the world; the mind is Brahman. Meditate upon the mind! 7.3.1.

He who meditates on the mind as Brahman—so far as the reach of the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on the mind as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than the mind? "There is indeed something greater than the mind. "May the venerable sir tell that to me. 7.3.2
Thus ends the third section.

Volition is indeed greater than the mind. For when one wills, then one reflects; then one utters speech; and one utters that speech in a name. In a name, the mantras become one; in the mantras, the ritual acts [become one]. 7.4.1.

These, indeed, have *saṃkalpa* (volition) as their sole point of convergence, they consist of *saṃkalpa*, and they are established in *saṃkalpa*. Heaven and earth were willed together; wind and space were willed together; heat and fire were willed together. Through the willing of these, rain is willed; through the willing of rain, food is willed; through the willing of food, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are willed; through the willing of the vital breaths, the sacred hymns (*mantras*) are willed; through the willing of the sacred hymns, ritual acts (*karmāṇi*) are willed; through the willing of ritual acts, the world (*loka*) is willed; through the willing of the world, everything is willed. This is that *saṃkalpa*. Meditate upon *saṃkalpa*. 7.4.2.

He who meditates upon volition as Brahman attains worlds that are fashioned, stable, firmly established, unshakable, and free from distress; he himself becomes stable and free from distress. As far as the reach of volition extends, so far he has freedom of movement, provided he meditates upon volition as Brahman. "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than volition? "Indeed, there is something greater than volition. "May the venerable sir explain that to me. 7.4.3.
Thus ends the fourth section.

Mind, indeed, is greater than volition. For when one perceives, then one forms a volition; then one reflects; then one utters speech; and one utters that speech by means of a name. In a name, the sacred formulas become one; in the sacred formulas, the ritual acts [become one]. 7.5.1.

These, indeed, have thought as their single path, thought as their self, and are established in thought. Therefore, even if one is a man of great learning but lacks thought, people say of him, "He does not exist," for they think, "What he knows, or what he has learned as a scholar—he cannot be such a man without thought. But if one is a man of little learning yet possesses thought, people will listen to him with respect. For thought is their single path, thought is their self, and thought is their foundation. "Meditate upon thought! [7.5.2]

He who meditates on the mind as Brahman attains, indeed, worlds that are steadfast, being himself steadfast; he attains worlds that are established, being himself established; he attains worlds that are unshakable, being himself unshakable. As far as the reach of the mind extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on the mind as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than the mind? "There is indeed something greater than the mind. "May the venerable sir tell me that. 7.5.3.
Thus ends the fifth section.

"Concentration (*dhyāna*) is indeed greater than thought. The earth, as it were, meditates; the intermediate space, as it were, meditates; the sky, as it were, meditates; the waters, as it were, meditate; the mountains, as it were, meditate; gods and humans, as it were, meditate. Therefore, those among men here who attain greatness become, as it were, participants in the attainment of concentration. Now, those who are insignificant, quarrelsome, slanderous, and backbiters—they remain so. But those who are powerful become, as it were, participants in the attainment of concentration. Meditate upon concentration. (7.6.1)

He who meditates upon meditation as Brahman—so far as the reach of meditation extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon meditation as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than meditation? "There is indeed something greater than meditation. "May the venerable sir explain that to me. (7.6.2)
Thus ends the sixth section.

Consciousness, indeed, is greater than meditation. By means of consciousness, one discerns the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvaṇa* as the fourth, the *Itihāsa-purāṇa* as the fifth among the Vedas, the science of ancestral rites, mathematics, the science of portents, the science of treasures, logic and debate, etymology, the science of the gods, the science of sacred knowledge (*brahmavidyā*), the science of spirits, the science of governance, the science of the stars, the science of serpents and celestial beings; and one discerns by consciousness alone the heaven and the earth, the wind and space, the waters and fire, the gods and humans, cattle and birds, grasses and trees, beasts down to worms, winged insects, and ants; and one discerns by consciousness alone righteousness and unrighteousness, truth and falsehood, the good and the bad, the pleasant and the unpleasant, food and flavor, and this world and the next. "Revere consciousness. 7.7.1.

He who meditates on consciousness as Brahman attains worlds that possess consciousness and knowledge. As far as the reach of consciousness extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on consciousness as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than consciousness? "There is indeed something greater than consciousness. "May the venerable sir tell it to me. 7.7.2.
Thus ends the seventh section.

"Strength, indeed, is greater than consciousness. For even a single strong man can shake a hundred men who possess consciousness. When he is strong, then he is able to rise; rising, he becomes one who serves; serving, he becomes one who attends upon; attending, he becomes one who sees, one who hears, one who thinks, one who understands, one who acts, and one who perceives. By strength, indeed, the earth stands; by strength, the intermediate space; by strength, the sky; by strength, the mountains; by strength, gods and humans; by strength, cattle and birds, grasses and trees, wild beasts, down to worms, moths, and ants. By strength the world stands. Meditate upon strength. (7.8.1)

He who meditates upon strength as Brahman—so far as strength extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon strength as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than strength? "There is indeed something greater than strength. "May the venerable sir tell that to me. 7.8.2.
Thus ends the eighth section.

"Food indeed is greater than strength. Therefore, even if one were not to eat for ten nights—if indeed he should live—he becomes one who does not see, does not hear, does not think, does not understand, does not act, and does not discern. But through food, he becomes a seer, he becomes a hearer, he becomes a thinker, he becomes an understander, he becomes an actor, and he becomes a discerner. Meditate upon food. (7.9.1)

He who meditates on food as Brahman attains worlds rich in food and rich in drink. As far as food extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on food as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than food? "There is indeed something greater than food. "May the venerable sir tell that to me. 7.9.2
Thus ends the ninth section.

Water, indeed, is greater than food. Therefore, when there is no good rain, living beings become distressed, thinking, "Food will become scarce. But when there is good rain, living beings become joyful, thinking, "Food will abound. These material forms are nothing but water: this earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the mountains, gods and humans, cattle and birds, grasses, trees, wild beasts, down to worms, moths, and ants—all these material forms are water. Meditate upon water. 7.10.1

He who meditates on water as Brahman obtains all desires and becomes satisfied. As far as the reach of water extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on water as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than water? "There is indeed something greater than water. "May the venerable sir explain that to me. || 7.10.2 ||
Thus ends the tenth section.

Fire, indeed, is greater than water. Seizing the wind, it heats the sky; then they say, "It is glowing, it is scorching, it will rain. Fire, having first manifested itself, then creates water. Therefore, when there are flashes of lightning—both upward and across—and peals of thunder roll, people say, "It is flashing, it is thundering, it will rain. Fire, having first manifested itself, then creates water. Meditate upon fire. 7.11.1.

He who meditates on Brahman as splendor indeed becomes splendid; he attains splendid, radiant worlds from which darkness has been dispelled. As far as splendor extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on Brahman as splendor. "Venerable sir, is there anything greater than splendor? "Certainly, there is something greater than splendor. "May the venerable sir explain that to me. 7.11.2.
Thus ends the eleventh section.

"Space, indeed, is greater than fire. In space, indeed, are both the sun and the moon, lightning, the stars, and fire. By means of space one calls out; by means of space one hears; by means of space one answers. In space one rejoices; in space one does not rejoice. In space one is born; one is born from space. Meditate upon space. 7.12.1.

He who meditates on space as Brahman attains worlds that possess space, that are luminous, unconfined, and vast; as far as space extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on space as Brahman. "Revered sir, is there anything greater than space? "Indeed, there is something greater than space. "May the revered sir tell that to me. || 7.12.2 ||
Thus ends the twelfth section.

Memory indeed is greater than space. Therefore, even if many were to sit together without memory, they would not hear anything, nor would they think, nor would they understand. But when they do have memory, then they hear, then they think, then they understand. By memory one indeed discerns one's sons; by memory, one’s cattle. Meditate upon memory. 7.13.1.

He who meditates on memory as Brahman—so far as memory extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates on memory as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than memory? "There is indeed something greater than memory. "May the venerable sir explain that to me. 7.13.2.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

Hope, indeed, is greater than memory. For impelled by hope, one studies the sacred hymns, performs rituals, desires sons and cattle, and desires both this world and the world beyond. Meditate upon hope. 7.14.1.

He who meditates upon hope as Brahman—his every desire is fulfilled through hope; his prayers become unfailing. As far as the reach of hope extends, so far he has freedom of movement, he who meditates upon hope as Brahman. "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than hope? "There is something greater than hope. "May the venerable sir tell that to me. 7.14.2.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

Breath is indeed greater than hope. Just as the spokes are fixed in the hub, so everything is fixed in this breath. By means of breath one moves; breath gives breath; for the sake of breath one gives. Breath is the father; breath is the mother; breath is the brother; breath is the sister; breath is the teacher; breath is the brahmin. 7.15.1.

If he should speak harshly to his father, or mother, or brother, or sister, or teacher, or a Brahmin, they would say to him: "Shame on you! You are indeed a patricide; you are indeed a matricide; you are indeed a fratricide; you are indeed a sororicide; you are indeed a slayer of your teacher; you are indeed a slayer of a Brahmin. But even if he were to burn them all together with a poker after their life-breath has departed, they would not say of him: "You are a patricide," nor "You are a matricide," nor "You are a fratricide," nor "You are a sororicide," nor "You are a slayer of your teacher," nor "You are a slayer of a Brahmin. For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone becomes all these. He who sees thus, who thinks thus, and who understands thus, becomes a superior speaker (*ativādī*). If they should say to him, "Are you a superior speaker?", he should say, "I am a superior speaker," and he should not deny it.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.

"But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of truth. 'Venerable sir, may I speak transcendentally by means of truth? 'Truth itself, my dear, is what you must seek to understand. 'Venerable sir, I wish to understand truth. 7.16.1
Thus ends the sixteenth section.

"When one truly understands, then one speaks the truth; one who does not understand does not speak the truth. Only by understanding does one speak the truth. Therefore, understanding itself is what one must seek to understand. "Venerable sir, I wish to understand understanding. 7.17.1
Thus ends the seventeenth section.

"When one thinks, then one understands; one does not understand without having thought. Only after having thought does one understand. But thinking itself is what must be sought to be understood. "Venerable sir, I wish to seek to understand thinking. 7.18.1
Thus ends the eighteenth section.

"When one has faith, then one reflects; one who lacks faith does not reflect. Only one who has faith reflects. Faith, indeed, is what one must desire to understand. "Venerable sir, I desire to understand faith. 7.19.1
Thus ends the nineteenth section.

"When one has reached completion, then one has faith; one who has not reached completion does not have faith. Only by reaching completion does one have faith. Completion itself, however, is what must be sought to be known. "Venerable sir, I wish to know completion," [he said]. 7.20.1.
Thus ends the twentieth section.

"When one acts, then one attains completion; one does not attain completion without having acted. Only by acting does one attain completion. But action itself is what must be sought to be understood. "Venerable sir, I wish to understand action. 7.21.1
Thus ends the twenty-first section.

"When one indeed attains happiness, then one acts; one does not act having attained unhappiness. Having attained only happiness, one acts. But happiness itself is what one must desire to understand. "I desire to understand happiness, O Venerable Sir. 7.22.1
Thus ends the twenty-second section.

"That which is plenitude (bhūman) is happiness. There is no happiness in the finite; only plenitude is happiness. One must desire to understand plenitude. "Venerable sir, I desire to understand plenitude. 7.23.1.
Thus ends the twenty-third section.

Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (alpa). That which is the Infinite is immortal; but that which is the finite is mortal. "In what, O Venerable Sir, is it established? "In its own majesty, or perhaps not even in majesty. (7.24.1)

"Cattle and horses here are called 'greatness' (mahiman); elephants, gold, slaves, wives, fields, and dwellings are [also called greatness]. I do not speak thus," he said. "I do speak thus," he replied, "for one thing is established upon another. 7.24.2
Thus ends the twenty-fourth section.

He alone is below, He is above, He is behind, He is in front, He is to the south, He is to the north; He indeed is all this. Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the "I": "I alone am below, I am above, I am behind, I am in front, I am to the south, I am to the north; I indeed am all this. 7.25.1.

Now, therefore, follows the instruction regarding the Self alone: "The Self alone is below; the Self is above; the Self is behind; the Self is in front; the Self is to the south; the Self is to the north; the Self indeed is all this. He who sees thus, who thinks thus, who understands thus, finds delight in the Self, sports with the Self, has union with the Self, and rejoices in the Self; he becomes a self-ruler. For him, there is freedom of movement in all worlds. But those who know otherwise than this are ruled by others; their worlds are perishable, and they have no freedom of movement in any world. 7.25.2.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth section.

For him who sees thus, who reflects thus, and who understands thus—verily, from the Self comes breath, from the Self comes hope, from the Self comes memory, from the Self comes space, from the Self comes fire, from the Self comes water, from the Self come appearance and disappearance, from the Self comes food, from the Self comes strength, from the Self comes perception, from the Self comes meditation, from the Self comes thought, from the Self comes volition, from the Self comes mind, from the Self comes speech, from the Self comes name, from the Self come sacred hymns, from the Self come rites—from the Self alone, indeed, all this proceeds. 7.26.1.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"The seer sees neither death nor disease, nor even suffering.
The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every way. Thus it is said.
He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold, five-fold;
seven-fold and nine-fold, and again he is remembered as eleven-fold;
and one hundred and ten and one, and twenty thousand.

When food is pure, the inner being (*sattva*) becomes pure; when the inner being is pure, mindfulness becomes steady. Upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is the loosening of all knots. To him whose impurities have been rubbed away, the blessed Sanatkumāra shows the further shore of darkness. Him they call Skanda. (7.26.2)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth section.
Thus ends the seventh chapter.

Now, in this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-shaped dwelling; within it is a small space. That which is inside that [space] is what one must seek, and that indeed is what one must desire to understand. 8.1.1.

If they should say to him: "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space (ākāśa). What is there that is to be sought after, or that one should desire to understand? he should reply: 8.1.2. "What is there that is to be sought after, or that one should desire to understand? he should reply.
As vast as this space is, so vast is this space within the heart.
Both heaven and earth are contained entirely within it.
"Both fire and wind, both sun and moon, lightning and the stars—whatever he has here and whatever he does not have—all that is contained within him. (8.1.3)
If they should say to him: "If everything is contained within this city of Brahman—namely all beings and all desires—and when old age overtakes it or it perishes, what remains of it? [8.1.4]
He should say:
"It does not age with his aging; it is not slain by his being slain.
This is the true city of Brahman; in it, all desires are contained."

This Self is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst; its desires are true, its purposes are true. For just as here on earth people follow according to instruction, whatever end they desire—whether a country or a portion of land—they subsist upon that very thing. Just as a world won by action here on earth perishes, even so a world won by merit in the hereafter perishes. Therefore, those who depart from this world without having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is no freedom of movement in any of the worlds. But those who depart from this world after having discovered the Self and these true desires—for them there is freedom of movement in all the worlds.
Thus ends the first section.

If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him; endowed with that world of the fathers, he is magnified. Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of the mothers, by his mere volition the mothers arise for him; endowed with that world of the mothers, he is magnified. Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of brothers, by his mere volition the brothers arise for him; endowed with that world of brothers, he is magnified. Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of sisters, by his mere volition the sisters arise for him; endowed with that world of sisters, he is magnified. Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of friends, by his mere volition the friends arise for him; endowed with that world of friends, he is magnified. Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of perfumes and garlands, by his mere volition perfumes and garlands arise for him; endowed with that world of perfumes and garlands, he is magnified. Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of food and drink, by his mere volition food and drink arise for him; endowed with that world of food and drink, he is magnified. Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of song and music, by his mere volition song and music arise for him; endowed with that world of song and music, he is magnified. Then, if he becomes desirous of the world of women, by his mere volition women arise for him; endowed with that world of women, he is magnified.
Whatever end he desires, whatever wish he wishes for, that arises for him by his mere volition; endowed with that, he exults. 8.2.10.
Thus ends the second section.

These true desires have untruth as their covering. Of those true [desires], untruth is the covering. For whoever departs from here does not obtain them for the purpose of seeing them in this world. (8.3.1) Now, whatever living beings there are here of his, and whatever departed ones, and whatever else he desires but does not obtain—all that he finds by going there. For here indeed these true desires of his have untruth as their covering. It is just as if people who do not know the location of a buried treasure of gold might pass over it again and again without finding it; even so, all these creatures go day after day to this world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are held back by untruth. (8.3.2) That very Self is in the heart. This is its etymological explanation: "He is in the heart" (*hṛdi ayam*); therefore, it is called *hṛdayam*. One who knows this goes to the heavenly world day after day. (8.3.3) Now, this serene being (*saṃprasāda*), having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in his own true form. "This is the Self," he said; "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. The name of this very Brahman is "Truth" (*satyam*). (8.3.4) These, then, are three syllables: *sat-ti-yam*. That which is *sat* is the immortal. Now, that which is *ti* is mortal. And by *yam*, one holds both together. Because one holds both together with it, it is called *yam*. One who knows this goes to the heavenly world day after day. (8.3.5)
Thus ends the third section.

Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded. Neither day nor night cross this bridge; neither old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor merit, nor demerit crosses it. All evils turn back from it, for this world of Brahman is free from evil. Therefore, having crossed this bridge, one who was blind becomes non-blind; one who was pierced becomes non-pierced; one who was afflicted becomes non-afflicted. Therefore, having crossed this bridge, even night becomes truly day, for this world of Brahman is ever-shining. Those who find this world of Brahman through celibacy (*brahmacarya*), theirs alone is this world of Brahman; theirs is the freedom to move at will in all worlds.
Thus ends the fourth section.

Now, that which they call "sacrifice" (yajña) is simply celibacy (brahmacarya); for by means of celibacy alone does one who knows find that [Self]. And that which they call "the sacrifice performed" (iṣṭa) is simply celibacy; for having sacrificed by means of celibacy alone, one finds the Self. 8.5.1.

Now, that which they call "sattrāyaṇa" (the sacrificial session) is simply brahmacarya; for by means of brahmacarya alone one finds protection for the existing self. And that which they call "mauna" (silence) is simply brahmacarya; for by means of brahmacarya alone, having discovered the Self, one meditates upon it. 8.5.2.

Now, that which they call "the way of non-perishing" is indeed brahmacarya; for this Self does not perish, which one finds through brahmacarya. And that which they call "the way to the forest" is indeed brahmacarya. In the world of Brahman, in the third heaven from here, there are two oceans, Ara and Ṇya. There is the lake Airammadīya. There is the Aśvattha tree, Soma-savana. There is the city Aparājitā of Brahman, the golden hall built by the Lord. 8.5.3.

Therefore, those who find these two oceans, Ara and Ṇya, in the world of Brahman through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya)—for them alone belongs this world of Brahman; for them there is freedom to move at will in all worlds. 8.5.4.
Thus ends the fifth section.

Now, those channels of the heart—white, blue, yellow, and red—exist as [channels] of the subtle, tawny [light]. That sun is tawny; it is white; it is blue; it is yellow; it is red. Just as a great highway extends and goes to both villages, this one and that one, even so these rays of the sun go to both worlds, this one and that one. They extend from yonder sun and have entered into these channels; they extend from these channels and have entered into yonder sun.
When one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream, then he has entered into these channels; no evil touches him, for he is then endowed with light. 8.6.3.

Now, when he has been brought to such weakness, those sitting around him say, "Do you know me? Do you know me? As long as he has not departed from this body, so long does he know them. Then, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays. He passes away saying either "Om" or "Ho. As quickly as one could cast forth the mind, so swiftly does he go to the sun. This, indeed, is the gate to the world, the path for the wise, and the obstruction for the ignorant. Regarding this, there is this verse:
There are one hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head.
Going upward by that, one attains immortality; the others serve for departing in all directions, for departing in all directions. 8.6.6.
Thus ends the sixth section.

"That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that is what one must seek, that is what one must desire to understand. He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires," so said Prajāpati. 8.7.1.

Both the gods and the asuras became aware of this. They said, "Come, let us seek that Self, by seeking which one obtains all worlds and all desires. Indra went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from among the asuras. Without having come to an agreement with each other, they both approached Prajāpati with fuel in their hands. 8.7.2.

The two of them lived as religious students for thirty-two years. Prajāpati said to them: "Desiring what have you lived here? They replied: "It is reported that the words of the Blessed One are: 'That Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true—that Self is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known. He who, having found that Self, understands it, obtains all worlds and all desires. Desiring that [Self], we have lived here. (8.7.3)

Prajāpati said to them both: "This person who is seen in the eye—that is the Self," he said. "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. Then [Naciketas asked]: "Venerable sir, that which is perceived in the water and that which is perceived in a mirror—which one is this? He replied: "It is indeed this very same one that is perceived in all these ends. 8.7.4.
Thus ends the seventh section.

"Look at yourselves in a pan of water; whatever of yourselves you do not understand, tell that to me. They both looked into the pan of water. Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see? They both replied, "Venerable sir, we see our entire self here as a reflection, down to the very hairs and nails. (8.8.1)

Prajāpati said to them both, "Having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, look into a pan of water. They, having become well-adorned, well-dressed, and purified, looked into the pan of water. Prajāpati said to them, "What do you see? 8.8.2.

They both said, "Just as we two, O Venerable One, are well-adorned, well-dressed, and groomed here, even so these two, O Venerable One, are well-adorned, well-dressed, and groomed. "This is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. With their hearts at peace, they both departed. 8.8.3.

Having observed them, Prajāpati said: "They depart without having perceived the Self and without having realized it; whichever of them—whether gods or asuras—shall have this as their secret doctrine (upaniṣad), they shall perish. With a pacified heart, Virocana went to the asuras. He proclaimed this secret doctrine to them: "The self alone is to be magnified here; the self is to be served. By magnifying the self and serving the self here, one attains both worlds—this one and the one beyond. (8.8.4)

Therefore, even today, they say of one who does not give, who lacks faith, and who does not sacrifice, "Alas, he is an asura! For this is the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of the asuras: they adorn the body of the deceased with alms, clothing, and ornaments; for by this means, they think they will conquer that world. 8.8.5.
Thus ends the eighth section.

Then Indra, even before reaching the gods, perceived this fear: "Just as this [self] here becomes well-adorned when this body is well-adorned, well-dressed when it is well-dressed, and embellished when it is embellished; even so, it becomes blind when this body is blind, lame when it is lame, and maimed when it is maimed. It perishes following the destruction of this very body. I see no enjoyment in this. || 8.9.1 ||

With sacrificial fuel in his hand, he returned. Prajāpati said to him, "Maghavan, since you went away with Virocana having a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back? He replied, "Just as indeed, O Venerable One, when this body is well-adorned, one becomes well-adorned; when it is well-dressed, one becomes well-dressed; when it is embellished, one becomes embellished—even so, when this [body] is blind, one becomes blind; when it is lame, one becomes lame; when it is maimed, one becomes maimed. Following the destruction of this very body, this [self] perishes. I see no enjoyability in this. (8.9.2)

"It is even so, Maghavan," he said. "I shall explain this very matter to you further. Dwell for another thirty-two years. He dwelt for another thirty-two years, and then he said to him: 8.9.3.1–25.10.4.16 (Chāndogya Upaniṣad) "O Maghavan, this body consists of water; it is a mere dwelling-place and a resting-ground for that [inner self]. When a man departs from here, his speech merges into fire, his breath into wind, his sight into the sun, his hearing into the quarters, his mind into the moon, his physical strength into the lightning, his body hairs into the plants, and his blood and semen into the waters. Now, where does this person exist? Where does he abide? How does he return? Or does he not return? "If one has performed good deeds, one attains a similar state of being—either among the ancestors who enjoy what is given, or among the gods who subsist on truth, or among the gandharvas who possess both truth and desire, or among human beings who experience pleasure and pain, or among the demi-gods who subsist on faith, or among the celestial musicians who subsist on the essence of water, or among the gods who subsist on form, or among the gods who subsist on desire, or among the gods who subsist on what is produced, or among the gods who subsist on touch, or among the gods who subsist on sight, or among the gods who subsist on sound, or among the gods who subsist on the mind, or among the gods who subsist on bliss, or among the Brahman-knower gods who subsist on Brahman. Having attained such a state, he remains there as long as his merits last. When his merit is exhausted, he passes away from that state and returns to this world, descending again through the sequence of air, smoke, mist, cloud, rain, and earth. Having reached the earth, he becomes food. As food, he is offered into the sacrificial fire of man. From that, he arises as an embryo and is born again. This is the case for one who has desires. "But as for one who is without desire, who is free from desire, whose desire is satisfied, and whose desire is the Self—for him, all the vital functions merge into the supreme Self. There is no longer any coming and going for him. This is the end of his journey. Thus spoke Yājñavalkya. "This is the end of my journey," said Maitreyī. "This is the end of my journey," said Yājñavalkya. Then Maitreyī said, "Right here, sir, you have brought me into confusion. Indeed, I do not understand this. He said, "O Maitreyī, I am speaking only of the non-dual Reality. Where there is a duality of 'this' and 'that,' one sees the other, one smells the other, one tastes the other, one speaks to the other, one hears the other, one perceives the other, one touches the other, and one knows the other. But where everything has become the Self, then by whom and whom would one see? By whom and whom would one smell? By whom and whom would one taste? By whom and to whom would one speak? By whom and whom would one hear? By whom and whom would one perceive? By whom and whom would one touch? By whom and whom would one know? By what means would one know Him by whom all this is known? How could one know the Knower? Thus far extends the instruction of Yājñavalkya. Beyond this, there is only the teaching concerning the Great Path. "When a man departs from here, he goes to the wind. The wind opens up a space for him like an opening in a window, and through it he ascends. He reaches the sun. The sun opens up a space for him like an opening in a window, and through it he ascends. He reaches the moon. The moon opens up a space for him like an opening in a window, and through it he ascends. He reaches the world of Brahman. Having reached the world of Brahman, he becomes immortal, free from fear. Then Janaka, the King of Videha, said, "I shall give you, sir, whatever you desire. "That which moves about being honored in sleep—this is the Self," he said. "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. With a peaceful heart, he departed. But even before reaching the gods, he perceived this fear: "Even if this body becomes blind, he remains sighted; even if it becomes lame, he remains not lame. He is not affected by its defect. He is not slain when it is slain; he does not become lame when it is lame. Yet they kill him, as it were; they cause him to tremble, as it were. He experiences what is unpleasant, as it were; he even weeps, as it were. I see nothing enjoyable in this. || 8.10.1–2 ||

With fuel in his hand, he returned. Prajāpati said to him: "Maghavan, since you have departed with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back? He replied: "Venerable sir, even if this body becomes blind, he [the self] remains sighted; if it becomes lame, he remains not-lame. He is not affected by its defect. He is not killed by its being killed; he does not become lame by its becoming lame. Yet they strike at him as it were; they hide him away as it were; he experiences unpleasantness as it were; he even weeps as it were. I see nothing enjoyable in this. "It is exactly so, Maghavan," he said. "But I shall explain this further to you. Dwell here for another thirty-two years. He lived there for another thirty-two years. To him, he then spoke.
Thus ends the tenth section.

"Therefore, when one is thus asleep, composed, serene, and does not perceive any dream—this is the Self," he said. "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman. With a peaceful heart, he departed. But even before reaching the gods, he perceived this danger: "Indeed, in this state, one does not know oneself as 'I am this'; nor does one know these beings. One has simply gone to destruction. I see no enjoyment here. (8.11.1)

With fuel in his hand, he returned. Prajāpati said to him, "Maghavan, since you have departed with a peaceful heart, desiring what have you come back? He replied, "Indeed, venerable sir, even now one does not know this Self as 'This is I'; nor indeed these beings. One has gone to utter destruction; I see no enjoyment here. (8.11.2)

"It is even so, O Maghavan," he said. "I shall explain this very thing to you further, but not anything other than this. Dwell for another five years. He dwelt for another five years; thus they amounted to one hundred and one. This is what they say: "For one hundred and one years, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) with Prajāpati. To him, he then spoke. 8.11.3.
Thus ends the eleventh section.

O Maghavan, this mortal body is indeed seized by death; it is the support for that immortal, bodiless Self. For one who possesses a body is indeed seized by pleasure and pain. For one who possesses a body, there is no removal of pleasure and pain. But when one is truly bodiless, pleasure and pain do not touch him. 8.12.1.

The wind is bodiless; the cloud, lightning, and thunder—these are bodiless. Just as these, having risen from yonder sky and attained the highest light, appear in their own true form, even so this serene being (*saṃprasāda*), having risen from this body and attained the highest light, appears in its own true form. That is the Supreme Person (*uttama-puruṣa*). There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, with women, or vehicles, or kinsmen, not remembering this body which has come into existence. As a draft-animal is yoked to a wagon, even so is this vital breath (*prāṇa*) yoked to this body.

Now, where this space has entered into the eye, that is the person in the eye; the eye is for the purpose of seeing. Now, he who knows, "Let me smell this," he is the Self; the nose is for the purpose of smelling. Now, he who knows, "Let me speak this," he is the Self; speech is for the purpose of speaking. Now, he who knows, "Let me hear this," he is the Self; the ear is for the purpose of hearing. (8.12.4) Now, he who knows, "Let me think this," he is the Self. The mind is his divine eye. Indeed, with this divine eye, the mind, he sees and rejoices in those desires which are in the world of Brahman. (8.12.5)

The gods indeed worship that very Self; therefore, all worlds and all desires have been attained by them. He who, having discovered that Self, understands it, attains all worlds and all desires—thus spoke Prajāpati, thus spoke Prajāpati. 8.12.6
Thus ends the twelfth section.

From the dark I go to the speckled; from the speckled I go to the dark. Like a horse shaking off its hairs, having shaken off evil, and like the moon freeing itself from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, I—being one whose self is perfected—attain the uncreated world of Brahman; yes, I attain it. 8.13.1.
Thus ends the thirteenth section.

Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form; that which is between them is Brahman, that is the immortal, that is the Self. I enter the assembly hall, the abode of Prajāpati. May I become the glory of the Brāhmaṇas, the glory of the Kṣatriyas, the glory of the Vaiśyas. I have attained glory. I am indeed the glory of glories. O white one, non-biting; O non-biting white one, do not come near me; do not come near me, O slippery one! 8.14.1.
Thus ends the fourteenth section.

Brahmā told this to Prajāpati; Prajāpati told it to Manu; and Manu told it to his offspring. Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher according to the prescribed rule, and having performed the duties for the teacher during the remainder of his time, he should return home and, while living in his family, study his own portion of the Veda in a clean place, maintaining righteous conduct, fixing all his senses within himself, and not harming any living beings except at the sacred fords (tīrthas). Living thus as long as life lasts, he attains the world of Brahman and does not return again, he does not return again. 8.15.1.
Thus ends the fifteenth section.
Thus ends the eighth chapter.
Thus ends the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
